author: givros
text:
GPT-5.6 Pro is insane.

It didn’t just beat Claude 5, Fable and Mythos.

It crushed them.

One prompt, just 5 minutes. And voila:

A full low-poly Three.js island game with water, beach bar, boat, shark, fish, whales, sports area, NPCs and Ibiza vibes

This is getting ridiculous.

That is what I would write if I was not honest with you.

That is what I would post if I only wanted a viral clickbait tweet.

And this is exactly why you should always be careful with what you read on social media, especially on X.

There is no GPT-5.6 yet.

This prototype was made with GPT-5.5, in 6 iterations, after more than 40 minutes of back-and-forth with Codex.

Yes, it started with one prompt, and I will share that prompt below.

But the final result came from many corrections, adjustments, fixes, visual tweaks, Three.js issues, camera changes, object placement improvements, and a lot of manual direction.

That is the real workflow.

I share build in public content here to show what you can actually do with AI, but also to show that there is no magic dust.

AI is powerful.
Very powerful.

But the difference between a cool demo and a real usable prototype is still iteration, feedback, taste, debugging, and direction.

Yes, I am also waiting for GPT-5.6.

It will probably arrive next week, and when it does, we will test it here properly, in public, with real prompts, real iterations, and real results.

author: mysk_co
text:
Just out of curiosity, I let Claude attempt to port Loupe to Android using @skiptools. If you haven’t heard of Skip, it’s a tool that lets you produce native Android apps from a SwiftUI codebase. Loupe is written entirely in Swift and SwiftUI, so it should be a good match

This is the result after just one prompt (which was more or less like: port this app to Android using skip tools make no mistakes). The good news is that it actually builds and runs on device, the bad news is that pretty much nothing is functional yet. Claude recognised that it still needs to replace all the various native iOS frameworks for things like photos, location, and device motion with their Android equivalents, but for now it decided to defer all that work and just focus on getting the code to compile for Android

It’s still so surprising to me that this works at all. That said, I don’t think Loupe for Android is coming anytime soon since we have other stuff going on right now

author: kocer_eth
text:
THIS GUY BUILT A MINI AI DEV TEAM THAT CAN BUILD, VERSION, AND SHIP AN APP

not a “type one prompt and become a founder” thing

more like:

> Claude Code = junior developer
> GitHub = memory + version control
> Vercel = deployment button
> You = senior dev / product manager

that framing is the whole trick

most people use AI coding tools like a chatbot:
“make me an app”
then they paste errors for 3 hours
then they blame the model

better workflow:

1. write a tiny product spec
what should exist, who uses it, what is out of scope

2. give Claude Code one repo
not a random chat window. real files, real context, real diffs

3. ask for the smallest working version
one page, one database table, one deployable flow

4. push every change to GitHub
so your “AI dev team” has memory and you can roll back when it breaks

5. deploy on Vercel early
because a local demo is fake progress until it runs on a real URL

6. make the next prompt a code review, not a wish
“find bugs, security issues, missing edge cases, and unclear UX”

this is why the video works:
it shows AI coding as management, not magic

you are not replacing the whole dev team with one model

you are turning yourself into the person who writes tickets, reviews diffs, ships versions, and keeps scope small

caveat:
this breaks fast if you skip GitHub, skip specs, or let Claude rewrite half the app without review

but for MVPs, internal tools, landing pages, dashboards, and weird little automations?

this is already enough to feel like having a junior dev sitting next to you

author: jamesbarlia
text:
To Our Friend, Joshua Baer

Late Tuesday night, Joshua Baer, Co-Founder of @StationDC_HQ and Founder and CEO of @CapitalFactory, died in a private aircraft accident near Laredo, Texas.

Josh was 1 of 1. Everyone who knew him, or even briefly met him, would agree with that.

He'd walk into the Capitol wearing a Star Wars-themed Capital Factory graphic t-shirt, American flag shoes, his little dog Stormy by his side, and a Limitless pin clipped to his collar. Who does that?!

Josh was a friend, mentor, husband, and father to three kids who were his world. He was the ultimate connector, relentlessly optimistic, a technologist, and a believer in people before anyone else was.

Josh and I began formally working together about two years ago on STATION DC. We both had strong opinions, but we always saw eye-to-eye about the mission. Help entrepreneurs win. And we were both incredibly impatient about it - we couldn't, and wouldn't, wait around. We were going to build.

That impatience was never more obvious than the last time I saw him. He visited DC last week, and we spent a night catching up at STATION DC before dinner. For three hours (not hyperbole) he showed me every website, product, and agent he'd built with Claude. He even showed me how he was building a digital twin of Stormy: you could upload a video of her and the software would predict what she was saying to him. A Carnegie Mellon grad and a technologist through and through, he told me, "this is everything I've ever dreamed of! All the things we thought computers would be able to do actually can happen now! It's like magic!" His optimism, excitement, and love of technology were infectious. He meant it, and it rubbed off on a lot of people. He invited me to join him in Cabo that weekend to build a product that we both think should exist and could improve STATION's experience for our members - I couldn't make it, but we put it on the calendar for a few weeks out.

Not long before, we had what should've been a difficult, awkward conversation about the future - and he made it feel completely comfortable. He told me he was there for me, ready to support me however he could. Then he texted me a list of people he wanted to introduce me to. That was Josh.

He cared deeply about STATION DC - it became his gateway to DC. He and I both wanted it to be the front door for startups to win in this city. After every visit, he'd remind me how awesome DC is, how excited he was about what's happening here, and how much he loved being at the STATION DC Clubhouse with members. He'd tell me these early days genuinely reminded him of those first days in Austin 15 years ago - that something real was happening in DC and at STATION, and how intoxicating it was. You could feel he meant it. He loved seeing the city win. And it goes without saying that Capital Factory was everything to him. It was an extension of him - every piece of that place.

Josh was shamelessly himself. He loved what he did. He had a lot of fun. He played to win. He wanted to help everyone along the way - and he did. And maybe most importantly, he made a lot of people feel things, and believe in themselves, because they knew he was in their corner. That's a life well lived if you ask me.

We're going to keep building this thing - and keep believing in entrepreneurs, in the future, and in technology being used to help us. Josh poured himself into helping people, and the optimism, belief, and give-first approach he led with are how we intend to carry his legacy forward.

Take care, pal. I'll see you someday soon. Most likely as a hologram or something - that's probably what he'd want anyway.

author: zeuuss_01
text:
HERMES RUNS ASYNC.
MOST PEOPLE RUN IT LIKE A SEARCH BOX.

7 levels between typing prompts and letting it work while you sleep.👇

LEVEL 1 - TYPE, GET ANSWER
prompt in, reply out. Hermes as a chatbot.
fine for quick questions — but that’s 10% of it.

LEVEL 2 - IT REMEMBERS YOU (SOUL.MD)
context survives across sessions.

your SOUL.md sets who you are, how you talk, what’s off-limits.

same prompt from two people → two different answers.

LEVEL 3 - COMMANDS THAT FAN OUT WORK

/background → kicks a job to the side, result drops in a panel.

/steer → corrects a running task without stopping it.

/queue → stacks the next job to fire when this one ends.

/model → hot-swaps mid-session. 

Sonnet to plan, DeepSeek to build, Opus to review.

LEVEL 4 - SKILLS, EACH ON ITS OWN MODEL

every skill becomes a slash command:
/competitive-research, /social-media-copy, /code-review

the move: bind a model to each.

research → GPT-5.5 (cheap, high volume).

code → Fable 5. content → Sonnet.

stop paying flagship prices for budget work.

LEVEL 5 - MCPs (PLUG IN YOUR STACK)

Gmail, Calendar, Notion, Slack, ClickUp.
“how’d the numbers shake out this week?”
Hermes hits ClickUp, weighs it against your goals in memory, answers from real data.

caution: every MCP dumps tools into context.

15 MCPs × 10 tools = 150 schemas every turn. keep it lean.

LEVEL 6 - SUB-AGENTS IN PARALLEL

delegate_task spawns sub-agents on isolated context, run side by side:
delegate_task(tasks=[
{goal: “find best industries for websites”, model: “deepseek-v4-flash”},
{goal: “stress-test it, find the gaps”, model: “gpt-5.5”},
])
each child runs its own session and tools. parent collects the summaries.

LEVEL 7 - IT WORKS WHILE YOU’RE GONE

/goal → an objective held across turns, judged after each, runs till done (20 turns default).

cron jobs → scheduled sweeps. morning briefs, competitor scans, weekly recaps.
/background → side jobs that surface when ready.

the flip: from “I ask, it responds” to “it runs, I review.”

WHERE ARE YOU?

1 → chatbot
2 → it knows you
3 → parallel commands
4 → right model per task
5 → wired into your tools
6 → sub-agents in sync
7 → runs without you

most people are stuck at 2-3.

the climb from 4 to 7 is where the saved hours stack.

drop LEVEL in the comments and I’ll send the advanced tiers with setup.

Full build: a 3-agent research department on Hermes 👇

author: scottybeamio
text:
THIS CHINESE GUY BUILT A SYSTEM WHERE CLAUDE BUILDS, TESTS, AND FIXES ITS OWN CODE IN A LOOP UNTIL IT'S ACTUALLY PERFECT

Most people don't realize their AI coding agent runs once and hands you whatever comes out, bugs included.

He built a system that doesn't stop until the code is actually correct.

Two specialized agents in Claude Code:

→ Builder Agent: only writes and fixes code.
→ Checker Agent: only runs tests, type checks, and linting. Reports exactly what failed.

They're kept separate on purpose. An agent checking its own code can't catch its own blind spots.

An orchestrator command chains them into a loop:

→ Builder implements the feature
→ Checker runs everything
→ All green? Loop stops.
→ Something failed? Sent back to Builder. Fixed. Checked again. Repeat.

The critical detail most people miss: stop rules.

Max 5 cycles. After that, a human steps in.

If a fix breaks something that was previously passing, the loop stops immediately. Without this, agents start weakening tests just to fake a pass instead of actually fixing the bug.

This is what an actual autonomous dev workflow looks like. Not one-shot prompting. A real build-test-fix loop with guardrails.

Bookmark this post. Full setup is in the video below.

author: iam_elias1
text:
There has been a lot of hype around GLM 5.2 this week.

Most of it is deserved. Some of it is not.

Here is the honest breakdown what it actually is, and exactly how to use it for free.

GLM-5.2 was built by Zhipu AI, now called Z .ai, a company spun out of Tsinghua University in China. It launched June 13, 2026. The open weights went public on Hugging Face June 16-17.

Start with the claim that matters most.

According to Artificial Analysis, an independent AI research firm, GLM-5.2 is currently the #1 open-weights AI model in the world and 4th best overall, behind only a couple of OpenAI and Anthropic models.

That part of the hype is real. And unlike the models ahead of it, you can download this one and run it yourself. For free. With no licensing fees, ever.

Here is what genuinely deserves the attention.

MIT licensed with no regional restrictions. Self-host it, fine-tune it, deploy it commercially, zero limitations. A truly usable 1 million token context window, one of the largest of any open model. Two reasoning modes, High and Max. And cloud API pricing roughly 10x cheaper than Claude or GPT-5.

Now here is how to actually use it for free three ways, easiest to most technical.

Method 1: Z .ai directly. Go to z .ai. GLM-5.2 powers the chat interface. Start using it in your browser immediately. No install, no setup. The fastest way to test it. One warning server congestion at launch caused timeouts for a lot of users. If it is slow, wait a day or use the next method.

Method 2: OpenRouter. If you do not want to route data through Z .ai's servers, OpenRouter hosts GLM-5.2 through third-party providers. Sign up, get an API key, and use the low-cost or free-tier access. Best option for developers who want API access without the data routing concern.

Method 3: Self-host the weights. The weights are on Hugging Face under MIT license. Download, run on your own hardware, and your data never leaves your machine. The catch: it is a large model roughly 744B total parameters, around 40B active. You realistically need serious GPU hardware, around 8x H100 80GB or equivalent. Not a laptop job. But for enterprises, fully private deployment costs nothing in licensing.

It also works as a drop-in Claude Code replacement, plugs into Claude Code, Cline, OpenCode, Goose, and other OpenAI-compatible CLIs by overriding the base URL and model name.

Now here is the part of the hype that is not deserved, the honest caveats.

GLM-5.2 is not the single best AI model in the world. Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 still score higher overall. Anyone telling you it beats every model is overselling it.

It is text-only. For images or video in the GLM family, you need GLM-4.6V.

And there is real context behind the launch. Zhipu released GLM-5.2 as a direct response to US export controls, specifically the directive that forced Anthropic to block foreign access to its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models within 48 hours. The founder framed it as a stance: "the path to AGI must never be enclosed by high walls."

If you use the cloud API, you are routing data through servers operated by a Chinese company. For anything sensitive, self-hosting is the right path. Know that before you wire it into something important.

Here is the honest bottom line.

GLM-5.2 is not the best model on the planet. But it is the best one you can download, run privately, and use commercially for free with a 1 million token context window, at the exact moment the most powerful Western models are being locked behind export controls.

The hype overshoots on "best model ever."

It undersells on "free frontier intelligence you actually own."

The second one is the real story.

Source: Zhipu AI / Z .ai · Artificial Analysis · Pandaily · SuperCareer · June 13-17, 2026

quotedTweet.text:
GPT-5.6 vs GPT-5.5 on my custom spaceship prompt.

I gave both models the exact same custom prompt. This is also the same prompt I previously gave to Fable 5.

For context, GPT-5.6 Pro worked for 87 minutes, while GPT-5.5 Extra High worked for 34 minutes and 42 seconds.

As I’ve said before, based on great authority GPT-5.6 will be an incremental/soldi improvement over GPT-5.5, not a “Fable killer.” My rough expectation has been that it would trade blows with Fable 5 on some benchmarks, maybe win around half depending on the category, but not clearly surpass it overall. And again fable five will have bigger model smell, but this was expected.

After testing this coding output, that view feels pretty accurate.

GPT-5.6 is clearly better than GPT-5.5 in several visual areas. The lighting, shading, chairs, object details, and exterior of the spaceship looked noticeably stronger. The scene was also easier to test.

I do want to give GPT-5.5 credit though. It built out the rooms much much better and the planets looked better than GPT-5.6’s. It was also interesting that both GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 produced better-looking planets than Fable 5 in this specific test.

The downside with GPT-5.5 was stability. The game was much glitchier and harder to test compared to GPT-5.6.

But when it comes to the core of the demo, which is the spaceship itself, Fable 5 still beat both models pretty comfortably. GPT-5.6 is impressive, but from this test, it looks exactly like what I expected which was a meaningful incremental improvement over GPT-5.5, at least for indie game demos, but not something that replaces Fable 5.

In collaboration with @chetaslua

text:
順便一提。

想測試一個模型是否真正具備 Fable 5 「長時程自主完成複雜任務」的能力，最簡單直接的實驗場景是：

請模型把「你現實中最想去的具體地點」做成一個美觀、有氛圍的 three.js 互動虛擬景觀網頁。

要求：
- 玩家可以用滑鼠/鍵盤自由移動、旋轉視角
- 有適當的光影與大氣效果
- 場景要能傳達出該地點的真實氛圍

以上基本能一次验证 Anthropic 官方强调的 Fable 5 所有核心能力。

因爲 Fable 會自主研究真實地點，找到這個地點所有相關的數據，再去做創意轉化 + 技術實現，一次造出高质量的作品。其他模型暫時都不能做到~

因爲 Fable 會自主研究真實地點，找到這個地點所有相關的數據，再去做創意轉化 + 技術實現，一次造出高质量的作品。其他模型暫時都不能做到~

quotedTweet.text:
當我們在用 Fable 5 的時候，我們到底在用什麼？

昨天試著讓 Opus 4.8 接力把這東西修下去，結果人差點累廢了（😇

幾乎通宵，把 X 上流傳的、想讓 Opus 4.8 像 Fable 5 那樣超長工作的方法都跑了一遍，比如Pliny 發的那份所謂洩露的 system prompt，還有好些人試的提煉 session，全試了…… 之前忙於如何實現工具，沒有思考過更底層的問題，因此也算對 A 社的產品多了點理解。

btw Pliny 那份洩露的是 Chat / App 的系統提示詞，不是 agentic 腳手架那套，拿來讓 Opus 做長程 agent 工作完全不靠譜，這東西靠譜用法還是 Pliny 沒直接公開的多 agent 解構／重組工作流，搞越獄。

反正，結論是：（至少對這種大型複雜任務）都沒用。

靠有限的時間和訊息，試圖把強模型的行為一致性歸納出來，做成外部工程，想讓弱模型逼近強模型，對這種要長時間把控全局的任務，完全不現實。

同一個任務，Fable 5 能長時間獨立做完、幾乎不用人介入；換成上面這些方法讓 Opus 4.8 來硬凑，耗時十幾倍起步，錯誤百出，只能靠人腦不斷介入、統籌全局。

歸根到底，這兩個模型在把控空間的全局一致性上，能力差異是天壤之別。Fable 5 就是強太多，沒話説。

「用 Opus 在 100 小時內能完成的工作，用 Fable 可以在 1 小時內完成。」—— 這麽説，一點也不誇張。

Fable 本質是一種新 agent 工作流範式，新的 agent 工作流範式，意味著使用者要用新的思考方式去對待任務，不管以後還能不能用，好歹是提前體驗了一把未來一部分該有的樣子，知道該往哪些方向繼續卷了~

author: xmyttle
text:
THIS IS THE PART OF CLAUDE CODE MOST PEOPLE STILL MISUSE

they keep opening one session and treating it like a freelancer.

one prompt has to:
- research
- write
- edit
- judge
- remember context
- catch its own weak logic

that is why the output turns gray.

not because Claude is bad.

because the workflow is asking one brain to be the whole company.

the video shows the better pattern:
> route the task
> split the roles
> keep the context clean
> let each agent return one finished handoff
that is the shift.

Claude stops being a chat window.

it becomes a small operating team:
> one agent does research.
> one agent drafts.
> one agent edits.
> one agent reviews.
> one agent attacks the idea before the audience does.

a crew is not smarter because every person is a genius.

it is smarter because nobody is doing the wrong job.

author: mlbear2
text:
【6月18日 夜のニュースまとめ】
・Noam ShazeerがGoogleを退社しOpenAIへ移籍
・Midjourneyが初の医療ハードウェアを発表
・米政府がSK Telecom懸念でAnthropicに輸出規制
・金融大手の香港でのClaude遮断が拡大
・Unreal Engine 5.8がMCPサーバーを実験的サポート
・BigQueryの自律型エンベディング生成機能が一般提供
・リアルタイム視聴覚モデルMaineCoon登場
・KaggleポケカコンペでPrivate Sharingの懸念
・CMUの研究でCursor導入による生産性向上が実証

===

Noam ShazeerがGoogleを退社しOpenAIへ移籍

・Transformerの共同著者であり、Google DeepMindでGeminiの共同リーダーを務めていたNoam Shazeer氏がGoogleを退社し、OpenAIに移籍することが発表されました。
・OpenAIではアーキテクチャリサーチのリードに就任する予定であり、Sam Altman氏も歓迎の意を表明しています。
・GoogleにとってはGemini開発における大きな痛手となる一方、OpenAIのさらなる開発加速が期待され、今年最大のAI人材の移動として大きな話題を呼んでいます。

===

Midjourneyが初の医療ハードウェアを発表

・画像生成AIで知られるMidjourneyが、初のハードウェアプロジェクトとしてMidjourney Medicalを発表しました。
・全身を超音波でスキャンする機器を開発しており、MRIよりも安価で高速な医療スキャンを目指しています。
・2027年にはサンフランシスコにスパ施設をオープンする計画も明かされ、AI企業による予想外の医療・ヘルスケア分野への進出に驚きの声が上がっています。

===

米政府がSK Telecom懸念でAnthropicに輸出規制【続報】

・Anthropicのサイバーセキュリティモデル「Mythos」に関する続報です。
・ホワイトハウスが同モデルに対する輸出管理を課したことが報じられました。
・韓国の通信大手SK Telecomが同モデルへアクセスすることに対し、同社と中国との繋がりを懸念したことが背景にあるとされています。
・開発者からは、SK Telecomは中国の通信機器を使用していないとの指摘もあり、米政府の強硬な姿勢に波紋が広がっています。

===

金融大手の香港でのClaude遮断が拡大【続報】

・ウォール街の金融大手による香港でのClaude利用制限に関する続報です。
・Goldman Sachsに続き、JPMorgan Chaseなども香港の従業員によるClaudeへのアクセスを遮断したことが報じられました。
・米中間の地政学的な緊張が高まる中、コンプライアンスやセキュリティ上の懸念が背景にあるとみられます。
・金融業界におけるAIツールの利用制限が、地域によってさらに厳格化される動きとして注目されています。

===

Unreal Engine 5.8がMCPサーバーを実験的サポート

・本日リリースされたUnreal Engine 5.8において、MCPサーバーのサポートが実験的に追加されました。
・これにより、任意のAIエージェントをUnreal Engineのパイプラインやワークフローに直接接続することが可能になります。
・ゲーム開発におけるAIエージェントの活用が本格化する第一歩として、開発者から熱い視線が注がれています。

===

BigQueryの自律型エンベディング生成機能が一般提供

・Google CloudのBigQueryにおいて、自律型エンベディング生成機能が一般提供となりました。
・事前に設定しておくことで、特定の列が更新された際に自動でベクトル化し、別の列に追加してくれるようになります。
・設定や利用はすべてSQL文で完結するため、AI関数を用いたセマンティック検索などが容易に実装できると好評です。

===

リアルタイム視聴覚モデルMaineCoon登場

・Catnip社が、リアルタイムインタラクティブな視聴覚モデル「MaineCoon」を発表しました。
・22Bパラメータのストリーミングモデルであり、AIキャラクターをレンダリングのために一時停止させることなく、リアルタイムで画面上に表示し続けることができます。
・従来のターン制の対話から、常に存在感のあるAIキャラクターとのインタラクションへと進化させる技術として注目されています。

===

KaggleポケカコンペでPrivate Sharingの懸念【続報】

・Kaggleで開催中のポケモンカードゲームAIコンペに関する続報です。
・参加者間でルールの範囲外となる情報共有（Private Sharing）の兆候が見られ、コミュニティ内で注意喚起が行われています。
・一方で、提出デッキが公開される仕様であることから、いっそPrivate Sharingを許可した方が面白いのではないかという意見も出ており、議論を呼んでいます。

===

CMUの研究でCursor導入による生産性向上が実証

・カーネギーメロン大学(CMU)の新たな研究により、AIコーディングエディタ「Cursor」の導入効果が実証されました。
・Cursorを導入した807のGitHubリポジトリと、導入していない類似リポジトリを比較した結果、導入後1ヶ月で明確な生産性の向上が確認されました。
・コーディングエージェントを正しく活用することで、開発のアウトプットに大きな差が生まれることがデータで裏付けられました。

author: mlbear2
text:
【6月19日 夜のニュースまとめ】
・Claude Code v2.1.183公開とアーキテクチャ図解
・Claude EnterpriseにMCPコネクタの一括認証機能が追加
・NotebookLMにクラウドコンピュータ機能追加
・AIエージェント専用の自律型メールボックスが登場
・ASMLの最先端チップ製造装置が中国に流出した可能性
・AI Agent向け新ベンチマークAA-Briefcase発表
・Google AI StudioとCloud SQLの連携機能が登場
・KaggleポケカコンペにSpiralAI参戦
・M365 Copilotを標的としたAIエージェントへの攻撃

===

Claude Code v2.1.183公開とアーキテクチャ図解【続報】

・Claude Codeに関する続報です。バージョン2.1.183がリリースされました。
・autoモードでの安全性が向上し、明示的な指示がない限り破壊的なgitコマンドがブロックされるようになりました。
・また、Claude Codeのアーキテクチャを6つのレイヤーに分けて視覚的に解説した図解がコミュニティで話題を集めています。

===

Claude EnterpriseにMCPコネクタの一括認証機能が追加

・Claude Enterpriseの管理者が、組織向けにMCPコネクタを一括で承認できる「Enterprise-Managed Auth」拡張機能がベータ版として登場しました。
・Asana、Slack、Figmaなどのツールへのアクセスを組織全体で一貫して管理できるようになります。
・企業でのAIエージェント導入を加速させる重要なアップデートとして注目されています。

===

NotebookLMにクラウドコンピュータ機能追加【続報】

・GoogleのNotebookLMに関する続報です。
・セッション内でコードを実行できるクラウドコンピュータ機能が新たに追加されました。
・ユーザーの指示に基づき、スプレッドシートの自動クリーンアップや計算などをNotebookLM内で直接実行可能になります。
・先日のエージェント機能搭載に続き、自律的な作業能力がさらに強化されています。

===

AIエージェント専用の自律型メールボックスが登場

・AIエージェントが人間の介入なしに独自の受信トレイを登録できる「Atomic_Mail」がオープンアルファ版として公開されました。
・MCPやAgent Skill経由で接続することで、エージェントがメールを通じたワークフローを自律的に実行可能になります。
・エージェントが外部とコミュニケーションを取るための新たなインフラとして期待されています。

===

ASMLの最先端チップ製造装置が中国に流出した可能性

・米国政府が、ASMLの最先端チップ製造装置の1つが輸出規制に違反して中国に渡った可能性があるとして懸念を表明しました。
・ASML側はこれを否定していますが、AI開発競争におけるハードウェアの輸出管理の難しさが浮き彫りになっています。
・中国のAI技術の進歩を遅らせようとする米国の戦略に影響を与える可能性があります。

===

AI Agent向け新ベンチマークAA-Briefcase発表

・業界の専門家が構築した複雑なプロジェクトにおけるAIエージェントの能力を評価する新ベンチマーク「AA-Briefcase」が発表されました。
・Claude Fable 5が首位を獲得しましたが、タスクあたりのコストが$31以上かかることが判明しました。
・一方で、DeepSeek V4 Flashは$0.04で実行可能であり、モデル間のコストパフォーマンスの差が明確になっています。

===

Google AI StudioとCloud SQLの連携機能が登場

・Google AI StudioからCloud SQL（現在はPostgreSQLのみ）への連携機能が追加されました。
・自然言語の指示だけで、データベースを含めたアプリケーションの構築からデプロイまでを一気通貫で行えるようになります。
・開発のハードルを大幅に下げる機能として、多くの開発者から歓迎されています。

===

KaggleポケカコンペにSpiralAI参戦【続報】

・Kaggleで開催中のポケモンカードゲームAIコンペに関する続報です。

author: tukiyomiiori
text:
GPT-5.6のリークまとめ動画が来ていた。

観ていて思ったのは、Fable 5と同じような執拗さを感じたこと。

Minecraftでは地下まで作るし、Voxelアートでも詳細な部分や動きや光りにも拘っている。こういうこだわりと執拗さは、Fable 5で見られたものに近いのではないだろうか。

ただし、Fable 5に追いつけるかは不明だ。理由は二つある。

一つは、ハーネスの問題。Fable 5にはClaude Codeという、馬鹿みたいに機能がゴテゴテしたハーネスがあり、Fable 5はそれを華麗に使いこなしていた。対して、GPT-5.6が使うCodexは、ハーネスとしてとてもシンプルだ。
（というか、今回のリークはチャットのものなので、ツール利用などの能力は不明）

二つ目はキャラクターであり、この部分はFable 5というか、Anthropicが明らかに先行している。つい最近の中の人のインタビューでも言われていたが、Fable 5／Mythosでは「強強エンジニアの仕事を学習させていた」疑惑がある。
また、ユーザーに「察してくれると思わせる」ような対話能力は特別だ。GPTモデルでそれを可能にするのは難しいだろう。というか、OpenAIはそういうものを求めていない気もする。

---

総じて、私はとても楽しみなのだが、心配はコストだ。

単純にトークンの値段が上がるだけではなく、「GPT-5.6 Proでなければ性能を発揮しない」ということも想定されるからだ。GPTのProモデルは、伝統的に桁違いに高額だ。

author: aniketapanjwani
text:
How can economists best make use of /goal in Codex and Claude Code?

I made a video demonstrating how I converted Kirill Borusyak's (@borusyak) Stata/Python DiD imputation package with a ~15 hour Codex goal left running overnight.

Now, this is a task you can likely one shot: i.e. /goal convert this package to R, verify everything lines up.

However, I find it helpful to define the validation criteria up front rather than leaving it to the coding agent to decide.

In our case, an existing Stata/Python package are helpful for pinning down the expected behavior of an R  package.

In more complex situations, I also recommend using Codex/Claude Code to help you think of validation criteria which would be helpful for "goal"s and how to acquire those criteria.

In the video, I also demo my preferred way of using Codex and Claude Code together (using Claude Code from within Codex), as well using a skill I've made using ChatGPT Pro to get a review of some intermediate work.

Video here: https://t.co/o4gtFGWQ54
Kirill's paper: https://t.co/7vyi4zbHe7
Generated R package: https://t.co/qIUJicTt8N

quotedTweet.text:
【保存版】

Karpathyがこう言った😳

https://t.co/qiHvwbLfyM

「ボトルネックから自分を外せ
レバレッジを最大化しろ
少ないトークンを入れるだけで
大量のことが自分の代わりに起きる」

これを構造で実現するのが「ループエンジニアリング」だ

手で回すセッションでは
「次に何を実行するか」と
「出力を確認するか」の2つを
人間がやっている

ループエンジニアリングは
この2つをシステムに移す

構造はこの4層👇

・スケジュール → 何を実行するかを決める
・ループ(メーカー) → 実際に作業する
・チェッカーエージェント → 出力を採点する
・ディスクのファイル → 2つが共有する状態を保持

設計のポイントが4つある

(1) チェッカーは別エージェントにする
モデルが自分の出力を採点すると
失敗を見つけるより正当化する方向に動く
チェッカーの結果が次のメーカーへの指示になり
何も見つからなくなるまでサイクルが回る

(2) 停止条件はループ前に設定する
実行中に変えるとトークンを燃やし続ける
シンプルな例：主要な問題を修正して最終パスを1回
「全テスト通過かつlintクリーン」で終了

(3) 状態はコンテキストではなくディスクに持つ
モデルは実行をまたいで記憶しない
MDファイルが「何が終わったか」「何が残っているか」を保持する
これで数日後にループが再開できる

(4) 検証バーが低いほど安全に動く
バージョン文字列の確認や不足テストの検出など
退屈で反復的な作業は人間が離れていても任せられる
判断が重いタスクも、チェッカーが結果を確認できる範囲ならループ化できる

Claude Codeのエージェントが途中で止まる原因の多くは
状態設計の問題だ

コンテキストに依存した状態は
セッションが切れた時点で白紙になる

チェッカー分離・停止条件の事前設定・ディスク状態の保持
この3つが整ったとき
Karpathyが言った「自分をボトルネックから外す」が初めて成立する

text:
A lot of developers are sleeping on the value of open weight LLMs. Every time I raise the value of open source AI, there are a bunch of people who say nobody wants to host their own trillion-param model and open LLMs are nowhere near frontier closed AI.

1- You don't need to host your own model, you can use OpenCode with any of the leading LLM (GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-v4, etc.) and get high-quality coding agents at a fraction of the price of Codex and Claude Code.
2- You don't need Fable-level AI for every task. A model like GLM-5.2 is enough for 80-90% of the tasks.
3- We're still in the early innings of on-device AI. There will be a huge momentum, especially as AI labs jack up the prices of LLM tokens.

بيئة full-stack واحدة.
Promptين فقط.

GLM 5.2 أظهر قوة واضحة في الجانب البصري وتوليد العالم:
Three.js مع مناطق رملية وغابات وثلج

شفافية نافذة أنظف من نماذج أخرى

crafting table بوصفات planks
توليد خامات مثل الفحم والحديد والذهب
كهوف تحت الأرض
دورة ليل ونهار
أداء ثابت قريب من 60 FPS
الميزة الأوضح كانت في التصميم البصري وتفاصيل العالم.
Claude Fable 5 ما زال أقوى في منطق الكود والاستقرار العام، خاصة في التفاصيل الوظيفية مثل الحركة والـ sprint.

لكن GLM 5.2 كان أكثر جرأة في الإضافة، وخرج بتفاصيل لم تُطلب أصلًا مثل الكهوف وmob drops.

مؤشرات الصحة تظهر خلف inventory.
العناصر تنتقل مباشرة للخانات.
والزومبي أحيانًا يطير بعد الضرب.

لكن الرسالة واضحة:

النماذج المفتوحة لم تعد مجرد بديل رخيص.
بعضها بدأ ينافس في التصميم، السرعة، وتوليد التجارب المعقدة.

هل تختار النموذج المغلق الأعلى تكلفة؟
أو تركيبة مفتوحة أرخص تعطيك 80% إلى 90% من النتيجة بسرعة أكبر؟

author: teksedge
text:
Interesting how GLM-5.2 beat Fable 5 at web design. ⚠️ Fable 5  tried to be "creative" and it backfired. Is this a deeper problem?

Careful review by @Designarena revealed it won through consistent high-quality templates that avoid classic AI antipatterns which Fable 5 engages in when attempting to be creative. GLM-5.2 was also had extremely effective Tailwind usage in 91% of sessions, strong Chart.js/Three.js integration, and significantly more intricate, animated outputs with better typography and layout.

GLM-5.2 generates ~25% more code for more expressive results. While it trades some speed for quality, it crushes on human preference.

Being MIT licensed and way cheaper ($1.40/$4.40 vs Fable’s $10/$50 per 1M tokens) didn't hurt either.

text:
Open-weight models are now cheap enough and capable enough to win most work, even while closed models still win the invisible layer: judgment per prompt.

That is the real point. The draft already has the ingredients, but the current version slightly blurs four separate claims:

GLM‑5.2 is a major open-weight jump. True and supportable.
It still costs more turns than GPT‑5.5 / Opus 4.8 / Fable 5 for some tasks. Strong experiential claim, but needs sharper language.
Benchmarks miss something important. Excellent point. Needs a name.
The Fable 5 shutdown gave https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F a market opening. Very strong, but should be phrased as “helped create” rather than “gave,” unless you want a deliberately provocative take.

https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F’s own GLM‑5.2 release page on Hugging Face describes it as a substantial leap over GLM‑5.1 for long-horizon tasks, with a 1M-token context window, flexible effort levels, stronger coding, and an MIT open-source license. Its benchmark table also shows big jumps over GLM‑5.1, including Terminal Bench 2.1 rising from 63.5 to 81.0.  Anthropic, meanwhile, launched Fable 5 on June 9, called it its most capable generally available model, then marked Fable 5 and Mythos 5 access unavailable on June 12.  Reuters and The Verge reported that the suspension followed a U.S. government directive limiting access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 over national-security concerns.

1. Core thesis upgrade

Your current thesis:

GLM 5.2 is great, but you need more prompts than with GPT 5.5 or Opus 4.8.

Better thesis:

GLM‑5.2 narrows the capability gap, but not the judgment gap.

Even better:

GLM‑5.2 proves open-weight models can now do most work. GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 still prove that the frontier is not just raw capability — it is judgment density.

Best:

The next model war is not benchmark score. It is prompts-to-done.

That phrase, prompts-to-done, should anchor the post. It captures the whole thing.

Benchmarks ask:

Can the model solve the task?

Real users ask:

How many times do I have to steer it before it becomes usable?

That is the missing layer.

2. Name the thing benchmarks miss

Your line is good:

“Call it taste, instinct, attention to detail.”

Make it sharper by naming the class:

judgment density

Meaning:

How much correct intent, taste, prioritisation, self-correction and finishing instinct the model packs into each turn.

Other strong terms:

TermMeaningPrompt economyHow much useful work you get per prompt.Judgment densityHow much taste, prioritisation and correctness appear in each response.Turn taxThe extra prompting needed to get an open model over the line.Friction gapThe difference between “can do it” and “gets it done cleanly.”Intent compressionHow well the model infers the real task from imperfect instructions.Taste layerThe model’s ability to choose what matters without being told.Finishing instinctWhether it closes loops and polishes the output without nudging.Prompt-to-done ratioNumber of user turns required to reach production-quality output.
Best phrase:
GLM‑5.2 is closing the benchmark gap. The closed labs still lead on prompt economy.
That is very strong.
3. The “three or four prompts vs one prompt” point is the heart
This is your best observation. Make it more explicit:
The difference is not always whether GLM‑5.2 can do the task. Often it can. The difference is that GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 understands the shape of the task sooner. It makes fewer bland choices, catches more missing constraints, preserves taste better, and arrives closer to “done” in one pass.
That is the invisible advantage.
OpenAI’s GPT‑5.5 system card says GPT‑5.5 is designed for complex real-world work and, relative to earlier models, “understands the task earlier,” asks for less guidance, uses tools more effectively, checks its work and keeps going until done.  Anthropic’s Opus 4.8 launch similarly foregrounded judgment: early testers said it asks better questions, catches its own mistakes, pushes back when a plan is unsound, and flags uncertainty more reliably.

That gives you the perfect support for the argument:

The closed labs still win because they reduce the number of steering interventions.

4. Stronger opening

Original:

GLM 5.2 is a massive jump from GLM 5.1.

Better:

GLM‑5.2 is a massive jump. But the real story is not the benchmark jump — it is the turn tax.

Or:

GLM‑5.2 is the first open-weight model in a while that made me change my routing. But it still has a hidden cost: prompts.

Or best:

GLM‑5.2 is good enough to change the model market. It is not yet good enough to erase the judgment gap.

That opening has tension.

5. Best rewritten version

GLM‑5.2 is a massive jump from GLM‑5.1.But there is a tradeoff people are not talking about: the turn tax.GLM‑5.2 can often accomplish the work. The issue is that you may need three or four prompts to get what GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 would often land in one.That gap does not always show up cleanly on benchmarks. Benchmarks measure whether a model can solve a task. Real work measures how much steering it needs before the output becomes https://t.co/DebLt40L8l it taste. Call it instinct. Call it attention to detail. I think the better name is judgment density: the ability to infer what matters, make the right default choices, preserve context, catch edge cases, and finish the job without being hand-held.Closed labs still have more of that.But the shift is real. We are entering an era where cheaper open-weight models can handle most everyday work. Fable 5 was overkill for 80% of vibe-coding tasks anyway. GLM‑5.2 does not need to be the best model in the world to be the model people use all day.And the timing matters. The Fable 5 shutdown created a sudden gap in the market. https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F walked straight through it.The lesson should be obvious: when you remove the best closed model from the hands of builders, you do not stop capability diffusion. You accelerate substitution.Restore Fable 5.

6. More aggressive version

GLM‑5.2 is not Fable 5. That is not the point.The point is that it is now close enough for most work and cheap enough to become default infrastructure.Yes, there is still a judgment gap. You can feel it immediately. GLM‑5.2 often needs three or four prompts to do what GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 lands in https://t.co/yLcY53IWI3 misses small intent. It needs more steering. It has less taste. It does not always know which detail matters before you tell it.But that is not the same as being unusable. That is the https://t.co/4zj9N4gqan models do not have to beat frontier closed models everywhere. They only have to be good enough, cheap enough, available enough and uncensored enough for builders to route real work through them.Fable 5 was overkill for most vibe coding. GLM‑5.2 is enough for most of it.The U.S. government did not kill demand by forcing Fable 5 offline. It redirected demand.GLM‑5.2 walked into the vacuum.Unban Fable 5.

7. More measured, credible version

GLM‑5.2 is a major open-weight jump, but it also exposes the part of model quality benchmarks still https://t.co/us7jh4dTP5 raw capability, the gap is shrinking fast. GLM‑5.2 can handle a lot of real coding and agentic work that would have been unrealistic for open models not long ago.But in use, there is still a difference between “can solve” and “gets it right in one pass.” GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 often have better prompt economy: they infer intent sooner, preserve taste better, notice missing constraints, and require fewer steering turns.That invisible layer — taste, instinct, attention to detail, judgment density — is where the closed labs still lead.But the market shift is obvious. Cheaper open-weight models do not need to beat frontier models outright. They only need to handle 80% of real work well enough. GLM‑5.2 may be the clearest sign yet that they can.The Fable 5 shutdown could not have been better timed for https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F.

8. Strongest X thread structure

Post 1

GLM‑5.2 is a massive jump from GLM‑5.1.But the real story is not just benchmark score. It is turn tax.

Post 2

GLM‑5.2 can often do the job. The issue is that you may need three or four prompts to get what GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 can often land in one.

Post 3

That gap is hard to see on benchmarks. Benchmarks measure whether a model can solve the task. Real work measures how much steering it needs before the answer becomes usable.

Post 4

Call it taste, instinct, attention to detail, or judgment https://t.co/CKpB6WHum1 is the ability to infer what matters before the user spells it out.

Post 5

Closed labs still have more of it. GPT‑5.5 and Opus 4.8 are often better at understanding the task earlier, pushing through ambiguity, catching small errors and finishing the work with less handholding.

Post 6

But the open-weight shift is real. GLM‑5.2 does not need to beat Fable 5. It only needs to be cheap, available and good enough for 80% of real tasks.

Post 7

Fable 5 was overkill for most vibe-coding tasks anyway. GLM‑5.2 is not as elegant, but it is good enough to change routing decisions.

Post 8

The Fable 5 shutdown created a market vacuum. https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F walked into it.

Post 9

The lesson: restricting frontier closed models does not stop demand. It pushes builders toward open alternatives faster.

Post 10

Restore Fable 5.

9. The factual/citation scaffold to add

You can make the post far more defensible by adding a small evidence spine:

https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F describes GLM‑5.2 as a long-horizon flagship model with a 1M-token context window and an MIT open-source license, and its published table shows large jumps over GLM‑5.1 on coding benchmarks like Terminal Bench 2.1.Anthropic described Fable 5 as exceeding any model it had previously made generally available, especially on long and complex tasks, but marked Fable 5 and Mythos 5 access unavailable three days after launch.GPT‑5.5 and Opus 4.8 are both explicitly positioned by their labs for complex professional and agentic work, where less steering and better judgment matter.

Then your opinion lands harder because the facts are anchored.

10. Important correction: “open source” vs “open-weight”

Your draft says:

Open source models are missing a level of intelligence…

For GLM‑5.2, “open source” is defensible because the Hugging Face page says “MIT open-source license.”  But in AI discourse, open-weight is often more precise. A model can have open weights while still not being “open source” in the full software sense of training data, training code, data filters, post-training recipes and eval harnesses.

Better:

Open-weight models are missing a level of intelligence that benchmarks do not measure.

Or:

Open-weight/open-source models are catching up fast, but they still miss the invisible layer benchmarks do not measure.

Best:

Open-weight models are closing the capability gap before they close the judgment gap.

That line is excellent.

11. Important correction: “US government gave https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F this opening”

This is punchy but a little too monocausal. GLM‑5.2 did not succeed only because Fable 5 was suspended. It shipped with real improvements: 1M context, stronger coding benchmarks, open weights, MIT licensing, and easy drop-in usage in Claude Code-like workflows. https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F’s own docs say GLM‑5.2 is live for GLM Coding Plan users and can be switched into Claude Code, including a 1M context suffix and effort mapping.

Better:

The Fable 5 shutdown did not create GLM‑5.2’s capability. But it created the perfect attention vacuum.

Or:

The U.S. government did not make GLM‑5.2 good. It made everyone look for an alternative at the exact moment GLM‑5.2 became good enough.

That is the best version.

12. Stronger “Fable 5 was overkill” argument

Original:

Fable 5 was overkill for 80% of vibe coding tasks anyway.

This is good, but you can make it more analytical:

Fable 5 was a Ferrari doing grocery runs for most vibe-coding sessions.

Or more serious:

Most vibe-coding tasks do not need the most capable model on Earth. They need fast iteration, cheap tokens, decent taste, long context, and enough autonomy to move through a codebase.

Best:

Fable 5 was not necessary for 80% of vibe coding. It was just nice to have because it collapsed the number of turns.

That connects back to the core thesis.

13. The “judgment density” section

This should be the intellectual centre of the post.

Write:

The missing capability is not just IQ. It is judgment https://t.co/CKpB6WHum1 shows up in tiny places:choosing the right abstraction without being told;
not overbuilding;
preserving the user’s taste;
knowing which edge case matters;
noticing when a spec is underdetermined;
asking one good question instead of generating three bad variants;
keeping the goal alive across edits;
finishing the last 10% without prompting.
Benchmarks rarely measure this because it is not one answer. It is how many interventions the user has to make before the work feels done.

That is a standout section.

14. The “turn tax” section

Use this:

The hidden cost of weaker models is not just tokens. It is turns.A cheap model that needs four prompts may still be cheaper in dollars, but it is not always cheaper in attention. The real unit is not cost per token. It is cost per completed decision.

This is excellent because it acknowledges GLM‑5.2’s value without pretending every task should use it.

Better still:

For many tasks, GLM‑5.2 wins on dollar cost and loses on human steering cost. The question is which cost matters more.

15. The routing framework you should add

Turn the post into practical advice:

Use GLM‑5.2 forUse GPT‑5.5 / Opus 4.8 / Fable 5 forroutine vibe codingambiguous product decisionsscaffoldingtaste-sensitive frontendrefactors with clear instructionsunclear architecture choiceslong-context codebase searchhigh-stakes reasoningrepetitive implementationone-shot strategic synthesischeap parallel attemptsfinal polishcode migration drafts“figure out what I mean” tasksbulk generationtasks where steering is expensive

Suggested line:

GLM‑5.2 is becoming the default worker. Closed models remain the architect, editor and taste layer.

That is very strong.

16. The “model stack” idea

This is a genius-level practical solution:

Do not think of this as GLM versus Fable. Think of it as routing.Use a closed model to define the spec, taste, architecture and acceptance criteria. Use GLM‑5.2 to execute cheap bulk work. Use the closed model again to review, compress and polish.

This is the near-term production workflow.

Call it:

frontier sandwiching

Process:

GPT‑5.5 / Opus / Fable writes the spec and acceptance criteria.

GLM‑5.2 executes the implementation.

GPT‑5.5 / Opus / Fable reviews the result and catches judgment errors.

Suggested paragraph:

The winning workflow may not be choosing one model. It may be using frontier models for judgment and open models for labor. Let the closed model decide what good looks like. Let GLM‑5.2 do the cheap passes. Then bring the frontier model back for review.

That is more useful than a model ranking.

17. The “benchmarks are measuring solvedness, not independence” point

Most coding benchmarks measure whether a model eventually gets a correct answer. But users care about independence.

Use this:

Benchmarks often measure solvedness. Builders care about independence.Did it infer the missing requirement?
Did it avoid the dumb default?
Did it notice the visual mismatch?
Did it preserve the concept through revisions?
Did it stop at the right level of complexity?
Did it know when not to touch something?
Did it finish without being babysat?

That is a key distinction.

18. The “one prompt vs four prompts” benchmark idea

Propose a new benchmark:

Prompts-to-Production

Metric:

Give models the same messy user request. Measure how many user interventions are required before a human evaluator would ship the output.

Subscores:
first-pass usefulness
number of clarification turns
number of correction turns
number of taste fixes
number of bug fixes
number of regressions introduced
final acceptance time

user cognitive load

Suggested wording:

We need benchmarks that score not just final answer quality, but intervention count. A model that reaches 90% after one prompt is not equivalent to a model that reaches 90% after four.

That is exactly your argument.

19. Obscure thought input: “the last-mile cognition gap”

This is what GLM‑5.2 may still lack.

Open models are increasingly good at the first 80% and surprisingly good at the next 10%. The last 10% is where frontier labs still earn their money: taste, defaults, edge cases, cohesion, and knowing when the answer is finished.

Line:

The intelligence gap has moved from “can it do the task?” to “can it finish without making me manage the task?”

That is excellent.

20. Obscure thought input: “defaults are intelligence”

This is one of the best deeper ideas.
Open models often fail not because they cannot follow instructions, but because they choose weaker defaults when instructions are incomplete.
Use:
A lot of frontier-model intelligence lives in defaults. When the user underspecifies, what does the model assume? Does it choose the tasteful layout, the safer architecture, the cleaner abstraction, the narrower scope, the more useful answer? That is where closed models still feel ahead.
That is exactly the invisible quality.
21. Obscure thought input: “taste is compressed experience”
This is strong:
Taste is not vibes. Taste is compressed experience. It is knowing which detail will matter later.
Expanded:

When people say a model has better taste, they usually mean it has internalised more examples of what good work looks like and can apply that pattern before being explicitly instructed. That is why it saves prompts.

22. Obscure thought input: “cheap tokens do not equal cheap outcomes”

This belongs in the post.

Cheap tokens are not the same as cheap outcomes. If the model needs more supervision, the user becomes the missing compute.

That is a killer line.

Another:

When the model is cheaper but needs more steering, the human becomes the premium token.

Excellent.

23. Obscure thought input: “availability is capability”

The Fable 5 shutdown makes this point:

A slightly worse model that is available beats a better model behind a policy wall.

Suggested paragraph:
In AI, availability is now a capability. A model can be objectively better and still lose workflows if it cannot be accessed, routed, automated or trusted to stay online.
That directly supports the Fable/GLM angle.

24. Obscure thought input: “geopolitical routing”

The Fable 5 ban created a sovereignty/availability problem. The response is not just users switching models. It is organisations learning to route across jurisdictions.

Use:

The Fable 5 shutdown taught builders a brutal lesson: model quality is not enough. Jurisdiction, export control, uptime, pricing, and political risk are now part of the model selection stack.

This is very strong.

25. Obscure thought input: “the substitution trap”

Governments may think restricting frontier models slows capability diffusion. But if the next-best alternative is good enough and open-weight, restrictions can accelerate adoption of less controllable models.

Suggested:
The substitution trap is that banning the best closed model can push users toward open models that are less governable, more portable and harder to recall.
That is a major strategic insight.
26. Better “Unban Fable 5” phrasing
“Unban Fable 5” is punchy. Keep it as a final line if the audience is builder Twitter.
But for credibility, alternatives:
Restore Fable 5.

Bring Fable 5 back.

Do not force the market into substitutes.

Put Fable 5 back under transparent rules.

Reopen Fable 5 with a clear, appealable safety framework.

Best practical version:

Restore Fable 5 under transparent rules.

Best viral version:

Unban Fable 5.
Use both:
Restore Fable 5 under transparent rules.Unban Fable 5.
27. Missing caution: Fable access was already going to change
Anthropic’s launch page said Fable 5 would be included in Pro, Max, Team and seat-based Enterprise plans through June 22, then move to usage credits on June 23, capacity permitting.  So avoid implying the model was guaranteed to remain freely available in the same form. The issue is not “it was going to be free forever and the government killed it.” The issue is access disruption and uncertainty.
Better:
Fable 5 was always going to be capacity-managed and credit-gated. The problem was not pricing. The problem was sudden access uncertainty.
28. Missing caution: GLM‑5.2 is text-only

Simon Willison notes GLM‑5.2 is a text-input-only open-weight model and that https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F’s separate vision family is not the open-weight GLM‑5.2 release.  This matters because if you compare GLM‑5.2 to Fable 5 on vibe coding and frontend, you should acknowledge that some Fable workflows involve vision or screenshot-based app reconstruction. Anthropic says Fable 5 can rebuild a web app’s source code from screenshots alone and has state-of-the-art vision capabilities.

Suggested wording:

GLM‑5.2’s rise is even more interesting because it is text-only in its open-weight form. It can rank highly on web-dev workflows without the vision loop that makes Fable 5 so strong.

That is a very good detail.

29. Missing nuance: “frontend” may be where GLM is better than expected

Your draft says open models miss taste and closed labs have more of it. That can coexist with GLM‑5.2 being surprisingly strong in web dev. Simon Willison notes GLM‑5.2 ranked second on Code Arena WebDev behind only Claude Fable 5, which he found impressive given the lack of image input.

So your sharper point is:

GLM‑5.2 can score highly on web-dev tasks and still require more steering in real workflows.

That is exactly the benchmark-vs-use gap.

Suggested line:

The paradox is that GLM‑5.2 can look elite on web-dev leaderboards and still feel less elite in a live session, because leaderboard solvedness is not the same as prompt economy.

30. Add a “where GLM‑5.2 wins” section

Do not make the post sound like a backhanded compliment. Give GLM its due.

GLM‑5.2 wins on:

price/performance;

availability;

open weights;

1M context;

routine coding tasks;

cheap parallelism;

local/controlled deployment for those with infrastructure;

drop-in compatibility with Claude Code-like workflows;

sovereignty and vendor-risk reduction.

Suggested paragraph:

The bullish case for GLM‑5.2 is not that it is the most tasteful model. It is that it is available, cheap, long-context, open-weight, and strong enough. That combination is lethal.

That is a great line.

31. Add a “where closed models still win” section

Closed models win on:

fewer turns;

better defaults;

visual/taste-sensitive frontend;

ambiguous requests;

preserving user intent;

self-critique;

not overengineering;

calibrated uncertainty;

one-shot architecture;

final polish;

agentic reliability across messy, long tasks.

Suggested paragraph:

The closed labs still win where the task is under-specified and taste-sensitive. When I know exactly what I want, GLM‑5.2 can be excellent. When I need the model to infer what good should look like, GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 still feel different.

32. Best “skeptic-proof” paragraph

Use this:

This is not a dunk on GLM‑5.2. It is the opposite. The fact that I am comparing it seriously to GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 is the story. The remaining gap is not raw usefulness. It is how much human steering the model needs before the work is shippable.

33. Best “open-source maximalist-proof” paragraph

Use this:

Open-weight advocates are right about the direction of travel. The gap is closing fast, and economics matter. But pretending the gap is gone does not help anyone. The frontier closed models still have a layer of intent inference and taste that shows up immediately in real work.

34. Best “closed-lab defender-proof” paragraph

Use this:

Closed-lab defenders are right that Fable 5 and GPT‑5.5 still feel more intelligent in high-ambiguity work. But they are wrong if they think that will protect the market. Most users do not buy the best model. They route to the cheapest model that gets them far enough.

35. The best “missing solution”: model routing, not model loyalty

Add:

The practical answer is not “use GLM” or “use Fable.” It is routing.Use GLM‑5.2 for cheap execution. Use GPT‑5.5 / Opus / Fable for spec creation, taste, review and final polish.The future is not one model. It is a stack.

This is the most useful recommendation.

The Fable 5 shutdown created a sudden gap in the market. https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F walked straight through it.The lesson should be obvious: when you remove the best closed model from the hands of builders, you do not stop capability diffusion. You accelerate substitution.Restore Fable 5.

6. More aggressive version

GLM‑5.2 is not Fable 5. That is not the point.The point is that it is now close enough for most work and cheap enough to become default infrastructure.Yes, there is still a judgment gap. You can feel it immediately. GLM‑5.2 often needs three or four prompts to do what GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 lands in https://t.co/yLcY53IWI3 misses small intent. It needs more steering. It has less taste. It does not always know which detail matters before you tell it.But that is not the same as being unusable. That is the https://t.co/4zj9N4gqan models do not have to beat frontier closed models everywhere. They only have to be good enough, cheap enough, available enough and uncensored enough for builders to route real work through them.Fable 5 was overkill for most vibe coding. GLM‑5.2 is enough for most of it.The U.S. government did not kill demand by forcing Fable 5 offline. It redirected demand.GLM‑5.2 walked into the vacuum.Unban Fable 5.

7. More measured, credible version

GLM‑5.2 is a major open-weight jump, but it also exposes the part of model quality benchmarks still https://t.co/us7jh4dTP5 raw capability, the gap is shrinking fast. GLM‑5.2 can handle a lot of real coding and agentic work that would have been unrealistic for open models not long ago.But in use, there is still a difference between “can solve” and “gets it right in one pass.” GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 often have better prompt economy: they infer intent sooner, preserve taste better, notice missing constraints, and require fewer steering turns.That invisible layer — taste, instinct, attention to detail, judgment density — is where the closed labs still lead.But the market shift is obvious. Cheaper open-weight models do not need to beat frontier models outright. They only need to handle 80% of real work well enough. GLM‑5.2 may be the clearest sign yet that they can.The Fable 5 shutdown could not have been better timed for https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F.

8. Strongest X thread structure

Post 1

GLM‑5.2 is a massive jump from GLM‑5.1.But the real story is not just benchmark score. It is turn tax.

Post 2

GLM‑5.2 can often do the job. The issue is that you may need three or four prompts to get what GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 or Fable 5 can often land in one.

Post 3

That gap is hard to see on benchmarks. Benchmarks measure whether a model can solve the task. Real work measures how much steering it needs before the answer becomes usable.

Post 4

Call it taste, instinct, attention to detail, or judgment https://t.co/CKpB6WHum1 is the ability to infer what matters before the user spells it out.

Post 5

Closed labs still have more of it. GPT‑5.5 and Opus 4.8 are often better at understanding the task earlier, pushing through ambiguity, catching small errors and finishing the work with less handholding.

Post 6

But the open-weight shift is real. GLM‑5.2 does not need to beat Fable 5. It only needs to be cheap, available and good enough for 80% of real tasks.

Post 7

Fable 5 was overkill for most vibe-coding tasks anyway. GLM‑5.2 is not as elegant, but it is good enough to change routing decisions.

Post 8

The Fable 5 shutdown created a market vacuum. https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F walked into it.

Post 9

The lesson: restricting frontier closed models does not stop demand. It pushes builders toward open alternatives faster.

Post 10

Restore Fable 5.

9. The factual/citation scaffold to add

You can make the post far more defensible by adding a small evidence spine:

https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F describes GLM‑5.2 as a long-horizon flagship model with a 1M-token context window and an MIT open-source license, and its published table shows large jumps over GLM‑5.1 on coding benchmarks like Terminal Bench 2.1.Anthropic described Fable 5 as exceeding any model it had previously made generally available, especially on long and complex tasks, but marked Fable 5 and Mythos 5 access unavailable three days after launch.GPT‑5.5 and Opus 4.8 are both explicitly positioned by their labs for complex professional and agentic work, where less steering and better judgment matter.

Then your opinion lands harder because the facts are anchored.

10. Important correction: “open source” vs “open-weight”

Your draft says:

Open source models are missing a level of intelligence…

For GLM‑5.2, “open source” is defensible because the Hugging Face page says “MIT open-source license.”  But in AI discourse, open-weight is often more precise. A model can have open weights while still not being “open source” in the full software sense of training data, training code, data filters, post-training recipes and eval harnesses.

Better:

Open-weight models are missing a level of intelligence that benchmarks do not measure.

Or:

Open-weight/open-source models are catching up fast, but they still miss the invisible layer benchmarks do not measure.

Best:

Open-weight models are closing the capability gap before they close the judgment gap.

That line is excellent.

11. Important correction: “US government gave https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F this opening”

This is punchy but a little too monocausal. GLM‑5.2 did not succeed only because Fable 5 was suspended. It shipped with real improvements: 1M context, stronger coding benchmarks, open weights, MIT licensing, and easy drop-in usage in Claude Code-like workflows. https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F’s own docs say GLM‑5.2 is live for GLM Coding Plan users and can be switched into Claude Code, including a 1M context suffix and effort mapping.

Better:

The Fable 5 shutdown did not create GLM‑5.2’s capability. But it created the perfect attention vacuum.

Or:

The U.S. government did not make GLM‑5.2 good. It made everyone look for an alternative at the exact moment GLM‑5.2 became good enough.

That is the best version.

12. Stronger “Fable 5 was overkill” argument

Original:

Fable 5 was overkill for 80% of vibe coding tasks anyway.

This is good, but you can make it more analytical:

Fable 5 was a Ferrari doing grocery runs for most vibe-coding sessions.

Or more serious:

Most vibe-coding tasks do not need the most capable model on Earth. They need fast iteration, cheap tokens, decent taste, long context, and enough autonomy to move through a codebase.

Best:

Fable 5 was not necessary for 80% of vibe coding. It was just nice to have because it collapsed the number of turns.

That connects back to the core thesis.

13. The “judgment density” section

This should be the intellectual centre of the post.

Write:

The missing capability is not just IQ. It is judgment https://t.co/CKpB6WHum1 shows up in tiny places:choosing the right abstraction without being told;
not overbuilding;
preserving the user’s taste;
knowing which edge case matters;
noticing when a spec is underdetermined;
asking one good question instead of generating three bad variants;
keeping the goal alive across edits;
finishing the last 10% without prompting.
Benchmarks rarely measure this because it is not one answer. It is how many interventions the user has to make before the work feels done.

That is a standout section.

14. The “turn tax” section

Use this:

The hidden cost of weaker models is not just tokens. It is turns.A cheap model that needs four prompts may still be cheaper in dollars, but it is not always cheaper in attention. The real unit is not cost per token. It is cost per completed decision.

This is excellent because it acknowledges GLM‑5.2’s value without pretending every task should use it.

Better still:

For many tasks, GLM‑5.2 wins on dollar cost and loses on human steering cost. The question is which cost matters more.

15. The routing framework you should add

Turn the post into practical advice:

Use GLM‑5.2 forUse GPT‑5.5 / Opus 4.8 / Fable 5 forroutine vibe codingambiguous product decisionsscaffoldingtaste-sensitive frontendrefactors with clear instructionsunclear architecture choiceslong-context codebase searchhigh-stakes reasoningrepetitive implementationone-shot strategic synthesischeap parallel attemptsfinal polishcode migration drafts“figure out what I mean” tasksbulk generationtasks where steering is expensive

Suggested line:

GLM‑5.2 is becoming the default worker. Closed models remain the architect, editor and taste layer.

That is very strong.

16. The “model stack” idea

This is a genius-level practical solution:

Do not think of this as GLM versus Fable. Think of it as routing.Use a closed model to define the spec, taste, architecture and acceptance criteria. Use GLM‑5.2 to execute cheap bulk work. Use the closed model again to review, compress and polish.

This is the near-term production workflow.

Call it:

frontier sandwiching

Process:

GPT‑5.5 / Opus / Fable writes the spec and acceptance criteria.

GLM‑5.2 executes the implementation.

GPT‑5.5 / Opus / Fable reviews the result and catches judgment errors.

Suggested paragraph:

The winning workflow may not be choosing one model. It may be using frontier models for judgment and open models for labor. Let the closed model decide what good looks like. Let GLM‑5.2 do the cheap passes. Then bring the frontier model back for review.

That is more useful than a model ranking.

17. The “benchmarks are measuring solvedness, not independence” point

Most coding benchmarks measure whether a model eventually gets a correct answer. But users care about independence.

Use this:

Benchmarks often measure solvedness. Builders care about independence.Did it infer the missing requirement?
Did it avoid the dumb default?
Did it notice the visual mismatch?
Did it preserve the concept through revisions?
Did it stop at the right level of complexity?
Did it know when not to touch something?
Did it finish without being babysat?

That is a key distinction.

18. The “one prompt vs four prompts” benchmark idea

Propose a new benchmark:

Prompts-to-Production

Metric:

Give models the same messy user request. Measure how many user interventions are required before a human evaluator would ship the output.

Subscores:
first-pass usefulness
number of clarification turns
number of correction turns
number of taste fixes
number of bug fixes
number of regressions introduced
final acceptance time

user cognitive load

Suggested wording:

We need benchmarks that score not just final answer quality, but intervention count. A model that reaches 90% after one prompt is not equivalent to a model that reaches 90% after four.

That is exactly your argument.

19. Obscure thought input: “the last-mile cognition gap”

This is what GLM‑5.2 may still lack.

Open models are increasingly good at the first 80% and surprisingly good at the next 10%. The last 10% is where frontier labs still earn their money: taste, defaults, edge cases, cohesion, and knowing when the answer is finished.

Line:

The intelligence gap has moved from “can it do the task?” to “can it finish without making me manage the task?”

That is excellent.

20. Obscure thought input: “defaults are intelligence”

This is one of the best deeper ideas.
Open models often fail not because they cannot follow instructions, but because they choose weaker defaults when instructions are incomplete.
Use:
A lot of frontier-model intelligence lives in defaults. When the user underspecifies, what does the model assume? Does it choose the tasteful layout, the safer architecture, the cleaner abstraction, the narrower scope, the more useful answer? That is where closed models still feel ahead.
That is exactly the invisible quality.
21. Obscure thought input: “taste is compressed experience”
This is strong:
Taste is not vibes. Taste is compressed experience. It is knowing which detail will matter later.
Expanded:

When people say a model has better taste, they usually mean it has internalised more examples of what good work looks like and can apply that pattern before being explicitly instructed. That is why it saves prompts.

22. Obscure thought input: “cheap tokens do not equal cheap outcomes”

This belongs in the post.

Cheap tokens are not the same as cheap outcomes. If the model needs more supervision, the user becomes the missing compute.

That is a killer line.

Another:

When the model is cheaper but needs more steering, the human becomes the premium token.

Excellent.

23. Obscure thought input: “availability is capability”

The Fable 5 shutdown makes this point:

A slightly worse model that is available beats a better model behind a policy wall.

Suggested paragraph:
In AI, availability is now a capability. A model can be objectively better and still lose workflows if it cannot be accessed, routed, automated or trusted to stay online.
That directly supports the Fable/GLM angle.

24. Obscure thought input: “geopolitical routing”

The Fable 5 ban created a sovereignty/availability problem. The response is not just users switching models. It is organisations learning to route across jurisdictions.

Use:

The Fable 5 shutdown taught builders a brutal lesson: model quality is not enough. Jurisdiction, export control, uptime, pricing, and political risk are now part of the model selection stack.

This is very strong.

25. Obscure thought input: “the substitution trap”

Governments may think restricting frontier models slows capability diffusion. But if the next-best alternative is good enough and open-weight, restrictions can accelerate adoption of less controllable models.

Suggested:
The substitution trap is that banning the best closed model can push users toward open models that are less governable, more portable and harder to recall.
That is a major strategic insight.
26. Better “Unban Fable 5” phrasing
“Unban Fable 5” is punchy. Keep it as a final line if the audience is builder Twitter.
But for credibility, alternatives:
Restore Fable 5.

Bring Fable 5 back.

Do not force the market into substitutes.

Put Fable 5 back under transparent rules.

Reopen Fable 5 with a clear, appealable safety framework.

Best practical version:

Restore Fable 5 under transparent rules.

Best viral version:

Unban Fable 5.
Use both:
Restore Fable 5 under transparent rules.Unban Fable 5.
27. Missing caution: Fable access was already going to change
Anthropic’s launch page said Fable 5 would be included in Pro, Max, Team and seat-based Enterprise plans through June 22, then move to usage credits on June 23, capacity permitting.  So avoid implying the model was guaranteed to remain freely available in the same form. The issue is not “it was going to be free forever and the government killed it.” The issue is access disruption and uncertainty.
Better:
Fable 5 was always going to be capacity-managed and credit-gated. The problem was not pricing. The problem was sudden access uncertainty.
28. Missing caution: GLM‑5.2 is text-only

Simon Willison notes GLM‑5.2 is a text-input-only open-weight model and that https://t.co/8l5VZLWr2F’s separate vision family is not the open-weight GLM‑5.2 release.  This matters because if you compare GLM‑5.2 to Fable 5 on vibe coding and frontend, you should acknowledge that some Fable workflows involve vision or screenshot-based app reconstruction. Anthropic says Fable 5 can rebuild a web app’s source code from screenshots alone and has state-of-the-art vision capabilities.

Suggested wording:

GLM‑5.2’s rise is even more interesting because it is text-only in its open-weight form. It can rank highly on web-dev workflows without the vision loop that makes Fable 5 so strong.

That is a very good detail.

29. Missing nuance: “frontend” may be where GLM is better than expected

Your draft says open models miss taste and closed labs have more of it. That can coexist with GLM‑5.2 being surprisingly strong in web dev. Simon Willison notes GLM‑5.2 ranked second on Code Arena WebDev behind only Claude Fable 5, which he found impressive given the lack of image input.

So your sharper point is:

GLM‑5.2 can score highly on web-dev tasks and still require more steering in real workflows.

That is exactly the benchmark-vs-use gap.

Suggested line:

The paradox is that GLM‑5.2 can look elite on web-dev leaderboards and still feel less elite in a live session, because leaderboard solvedness is not the same as prompt economy.

30. Add a “where GLM‑5.2 wins” section

Do not make the post sound like a backhanded compliment. Give GLM its due.

GLM‑5.2 wins on:

price/performance;

availability;

open weights;

1M context;

routine coding tasks;

cheap parallelism;

local/controlled deployment for those with infrastructure;

drop-in compatibility with Claude Code-like workflows;

sovereignty and vendor-risk reduction.

Suggested paragraph:

The bullish case for GLM‑5.2 is not that it is the most tasteful model. It is that it is available, cheap, long-context, open-weight, and strong enough. That combination is lethal.

That is a great line.

31. Add a “where closed models still win” section

Closed models win on:

fewer turns;

better defaults;

visual/taste-sensitive frontend;

ambiguous requests;

preserving user intent;

self-critique;

not overengineering;

calibrated uncertainty;

one-shot architecture;

final polish;

agentic reliability across messy, long tasks.

Suggested paragraph:

The closed labs still win where the task is under-specified and taste-sensitive. When I know exactly what I want, GLM‑5.2 can be excellent. When I need the model to infer what good should look like, GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 still feel different.

32. Best “skeptic-proof” paragraph

Use this:

This is not a dunk on GLM‑5.2. It is the opposite. The fact that I am comparing it seriously to GPT‑5.5, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5 is the story. The remaining gap is not raw usefulness. It is how much human steering the model needs before the work is shippable.

33. Best “open-source maximalist-proof” paragraph

Use this:

Open-weight advocates are right about the direction of travel. The gap is closing fast, and economics matter. But pretending the gap is gone does not help anyone. The frontier closed models still have a layer of intent inference and taste that shows up immediately in real work.

34. Best “closed-lab defender-proof” paragraph

Use this:

Closed-lab defenders are right that Fable 5 and GPT‑5.5 still feel more intelligent in high-ambiguity work. But they are wrong if they think that will protect the market. Most users do not buy the best model. They route to the cheapest model that gets them far enough.

35. The best “missing solution”: model routing, not model loyalty

Add:

The practical answer is not “use GLM” or “use Fable.” It is routing.Use GLM‑5.2 for cheap execution. Use GPT‑5.5 / Opus / Fable for spec creation, taste, review and final polish.The future is not one model. It is a stack.

This is the most useful recommendation.

36. Suggested benchmark you can propose publicly

text:
I built a backrooms horror game with claude fable 5, before it got banned.

the entire thing runs in your browser, no image files, no audio files, everything is generated by code.

→ the monster is procedurally modeled. no 3D assets, just math
→ it hunts by sight AND sound sprinting gives you away
→ stare at it and it freezes. keep staring and it charges you
→ the maze is different every run. 48×48 grid, fully connected
→ all audio is synthesized in the browser footsteps, whispers, heartbeat
→ a fear shader kicks in as it gets closer film grain, vignette, chromatic aberration

built with next.js, react, three.js, typescript, zero external assets.

author: ollobrains
text:
Google is not absent. It is compressing fewer, larger moves into the moments when everyone thinks it has gone quiet.

That is the real argument. The post should not sound like blind Gemini hype. It should sound like a market-pattern read.

There is one important factual correction: Google has released a Gemini 3.5 model since February — Gemini 3.5 Flash, announced at I/O on May 19, 2026. So the safer sentence is not “Google has not released a frontier model since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February.” It is: “Google has not released a new flagship Pro reasoning model since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February.” Google itself said on May 19 that Gemini 3.5 Pro was already being used internally and would roll out “next month,” which means June 2026 if that timeline holds.

1. Core thesis upgrade

Your current thesis:

Gemini 3.5 Pro is coming and might be the smartest model. Google ships less often but jumps bigger.

Better:

Gemini 3.5 Pro may be Google’s first real chance this year to retake the top intelligence narrative — not because Google has been inactive, but because it has been stacking work inside a slower flagship cadence.

Even sharper:

The AI race is not only about who ships most often. It is about who compounds the most between releases.

That is the argument. OpenAI and Anthropic have been visibly moving faster in public: OpenAI shipped GPT‑5.4 Thinking in March and GPT‑5.5 in April, while Anthropic released Opus 4.8 in May and Fable 5 in June.  Google’s counter-pattern is that its big flagship releases tend to arrive with broader multimodal/product integration: Gemini 3 launched in November, Gemini 3.1 Pro in February, and Gemini 3.5 Flash in May, with 3.5 Pro promised after internal use.

2. Best corrected version

Gemini 3.5 Pro is coming, and it has a real chance to be the most intelligent model in the world when it https://t.co/OFW0F5T0nH has not released a new flagship Pro reasoning model since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February. In that same window, OpenAI and Anthropic have shipped multiple frontier updates.But I do not read that as Google falling behind.I read it as Google’s https://t.co/mhhXmBv4AK releases less frequently at the flagship Pro layer. It trains longer, integrates deeper across products, and when it finally ships, the jump is usually meaningful.Gemini 3.5 Flash already showed the direction: frontier-level speed, stronger agentic coding, and performance that Google says beats 3.1 Pro across almost all benchmarks. Now the question is what happens when that 3.5 jump gets expressed in the Pro model.OpenAI and Anthropic are running a visible sprint. Google may be running a compounding https://t.co/pK2ZpLlvlY not count Google out.

3. More viral version

Gemini 3.5 Pro might be the model people are underestimating most right https://t.co/qtKVdr2sh2 has been quiet at the flagship Pro layer since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February. Meanwhile OpenAI and Anthropic have kept shipping.Easy read: Google is behind.I think that may be https://t.co/OqBCBGBinV’s pattern is different. It releases less often, trains longer, integrates harder, and then drops a model that suddenly resets the conversation.Gemini 3.5 Flash was the warning shot.Gemini 3.5 Pro is the real test.The monthly shippers are running a sprint. Google is running a different race.

4. More serious, journalist-safe version

Gemini 3.5 Pro may be one of the most important model releases of the https://t.co/tcpm7ygjdV has already released Gemini 3.5 Flash and said that Gemini 3.5 Pro is being used internally, with rollout planned after that. The current question is whether the Pro version can translate the 3.5 family’s gains into a true flagship reasoning model.The competitive context matters. Since Gemini 3.1 Pro launched in February, OpenAI has released GPT‑5.4 and GPT‑5.5, and Anthropic has released Opus 4.8 and Fable 5. Google has not matched that public cadence at the Pro layer.But slower cadence is not the same thing as weakness. Google’s advantage may be integration: multimodality, long context, search, Android, Workspace, YouTube, DeepMind research, TPUs, and product distribution.If Gemini 3.5 Pro combines frontier reasoning with that stack, it could be a serious contender for the top model slot.

5. The most important factual adjustment

Do not say:

Google has not released a frontier model since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February.

Because Google announced Gemini 3.5 Flash on May 19 and explicitly described it as a 3.5 model with frontier performance for agents and coding. Google’s model list currently shows Gemini 3.5 Flash as stable, alongside Gemini 3.1 Pro as preview.

Say this instead:

Google has not released a new flagship Pro model since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February.

Or:

At the flagship Pro reasoning tier, Google has been quiet since Gemini 3.1 Pro.

Best:

Google has not refreshed the Pro intelligence tier since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February. That is the quiet period that matters.

That one word — Pro — makes the post much more defensible.

6. Strengthen “coming”

Since Google officially said on May 19 that 3.5 Pro was being used internally and that it looked forward to rolling it out “next month,” your claim has a real official basis.  But as of the current Gemini API model list I found, Gemini 3.5 Flash is listed and Gemini 3.5 Pro is not visibly listed yet.

So write:

Gemini 3.5 Pro should be close. Google said in May that it was already being used internally and expected to roll out the following month.

Or:

Unless the timeline slips, Gemini 3.5 Pro should be a June release.

Avoid:

Gemini 3.5 Pro is definitely coming in a few days.
