author: y0tafomo
text:
Something just got smarter inside ChatGPT and nobody at OpenAI is saying anything.

This week alone, dozens of testers noticed the exact same thing 🧵

Across X, testers spent two days swapping screenshots and stopwatch times, all pointing to one theory: 

OpenAI is quietly A/B testing GPT-5.6 inside ChatGPT for some users.

The clearest signal is time, not quality.

One tester built a one-prompt 3D browser game with physics and camera controls. It took just over an hour — versus GPT-5.5 Pro's usual 10-minute mark.

Another tester said response times stretched to 20 or 40 minutes, a pace that hadn't shown up since before GPT-5.5 shipped.

Slower isn't always worse. Sometimes it means the model is actually thinking through something harder.

Not everyone is convinced it's a clean win.

One AI benchmarker ran the same spaceship-building prompt on both models. The suspected GPT-5.6 took 87 minutes against GPT-5.5 Extra High's 34 minutes — and Fable 5 still beat both on core geometry.

Leaked specs floating around are specific enough to feel real.

A knowledge cutoff pushed to December 2025. A reasoning-effort setting allegedly raised from 768 to 960. A release candidate nicknamed Kindle-Alpha.

Here's why the timing matters.

China's open-source GLM-5.2 trails Claude Opus 4.8 by just one point on a major engineering benchmark, while beating GPT-5.5 outright on the same test.

And Anthropic just handed every competitor a gap to fill.

Mythos 5 and Fable 5 remain pulled under a US export control directive, leaving the top of the market wide open.

Polymarket traders aren't waiting for confirmation.

Contracts on a GPT-5.6 launch between June 22 and June 28 priced as high as 89% this week.

The market already thinks this is real.

OpenAI still hasn't said a word.

author: ecnmic
text:
فکت چک:
ویدیو عمدتاً به نشت تصادفی کد منبع Claude Code آنتروپیک در ۳۱ مارس ۲۰۲۶ (۱۱ فروردین ۱۴۰۵) می‌پردازد و جزئیات فنی آن را به‌درستی توضیح می‌دهد:این نشت از طریق یک فایل source map (فایل .map با حجم حدود ۵۹٫۸ مگابایت) در پکیج npm نسخه ۲٫۱٫۸۸ از @anthropic-ai/claude-code اتفاق افتاد.
کد شامل حدود ۵۱۲٬۰۰۰ خط کد TypeScript (تقریباً ۱۹۰۰ فایل) بود که کلاینت‌ساید (client-side) ابزار کدنویسی هوش مصنوعی Claude Code را نشان می‌داد.
محقق امنیتی Chaofan Shou (@Fried_rice
) آن را کشف و عمومی کرد.
کد به‌سرعت در GitHub می‌رور شد، فورک گرفت و هزاران نفر آن را دانلود، تحلیل و به زبان‌های دیگر (مانند Python و Rust) پورت کردند. 
https://t.co/rAHHhuHS9h
آنتروپیک رسماً تأیید کرد که این یک خطای انسانی در packaging بوده، نه هک یا نقض امنیتی. هیچ داده مشتری، اعتبارنامه یا کد مدل (model weights) لو نرفته است. 
https://t.co/jLbBDPiVMI

ویدیو جزئیات واقعی مثل بیدار شدن محقق در ساعت ۴ صبح، نگرانی از اقدام قانونی آنتروپیک، و پورت سریع کد به Python/Rust برای دور زدن مسائل کپی‌رایت را درست نشان می‌دهد. این پورت‌ها توسط جامعه انجام شد (مثلاً reimplementation تمیز برای جلوگیری از مشکلات قانونی).نکات مهم درباره ادعاهای اضافیادعاهای نادرست یا اغراق‌آمیز بیشتر در متن پست (نه خود ویدیو) وجود دارد:زمان‌بندی اشتباه: نشت در مارس ۲۰۲۶ رخ داد، اما محدودیت‌های دسترسی ترامپ به مدل‌های پیشرفته آنتروپیک (مانند Fable 5 و Mythos 5) در ژوئن ۲۰۲۶ اعمال شد. نشت قبل از این رویدادها بوده و ربطی به آن ندارد. 
https://t.co/mO0HH79BIE
هک یا نفوذ اروپایی‌ها: هیچ مدرکی وجود ندارد. آنتروپیک و منابع معتبر آن را «خطای packaging» اعلام کرده‌اند، نه حمله سایبری.
بلاک‌چین: هیچ اشاره معتبری به قرار دادن کد روی بلاک‌چین برای «غیرقابل حذف بودن» وجود ندارد. این بخش احتمالاً ساخته‌شده است.

خلاصه: ویدیو در بخش فنی و واقعی نشت کد (کشف توسط Chaofan Shou، source map در npm، پورت به Python/Rust و انتشار در GitHub) صحیح و دقیق است. اما اگر پست همراه آن را هم در نظر بگیریم، روایت کلی (ارتباط با ترامپ، هک اروپایی‌ها، بلاک‌چین) نادرست و گمراه‌کننده است.

author: charels63430147
text:
You’ve simply acknowledged a few steps ahead of them: As long as AI capabilities continue to grow exponentially, its political destiny is essentially locked onto the same trajectory as nuclear weapons.

To put it in your style:
This script is nothing new; the path AI is taking today mirrors the path nuclear weapons took back then: open access first, followed by military control; a top-secret version kept internal, while a "safety-neutered" version is tossed to the public as a toy; and the rest is just a covert arms race between nations—haha.

Claude said:

That detail is worth verifying; let me check.
Searched the web

Searched the web

The facts are confirmed; let’s break it down systematically.

Basic outline of the event:
On June 13, Anthropic abruptly cut off global user access to "Fable 5" and "Mythos 5"—not due to a voluntary safety rollback by the company, but because of an export control directive from the U.S. Department of Commerce. TrueFoundry
The U.S. government ordered Anthropic to suspend access to these two models for "any foreign national"—regardless of whether they were located inside or outside the U.S.—citing national security concerns; the directive even applied to Anthropic's own foreign employees. Bloomberg
Anthropic received the directive at 5:21 PM Eastern Time, and the letter provided no specific details regarding the national security concerns. Anthropic understood the government's position to be that someone had discovered a way to "jailbreak" Fable 5. Anthropic

Looking back at your 2023 predictions, which ones turned out to be accurate?
Two things were spot on:
First, the emergence of a tiered system. Fable is public-facing, while Mythos—sharing the same underlying model—lifts certain restrictions for trusted users in cybersecurity and biology; this clearly constitutes a multi-tiered structure. Mythos 5 uses the same underlying model as Fable 5 but removes specific safety constraints for trusted users in cybersecurity and biology. Substack
Second, the government's determination to control frontier models is real. The US government successfully forced a tech company to take a model offline via a single letter—a process that appeared to require no court approval. TechCrunch

However, one aspect was more heavy-handed than you anticipated:
You had assumed that tiering would evolve through technical refinement—where different security levels corresponded to different capabilities.
In reality, the directive lacked specific written details. Anthropic’s interpretation—along with reports from Axios, CNBC, and NBC News—was that another company claimed to the Department of Commerce that Mythos could be "jailbroken," prompting immediate action from a government already wary of Anthropic. Explainx
In other words, the trigger for this intervention wasn't a rigorous technical assessment, but rather a report from a competitor combined with political mistrust. The control measures were cruder and more politicized than you expected, rather than being technically driven.

What is your take on the "tittytainment" (pacifying entertainment) theory now?
That assessment was structurally correct but needs refinement.
True tiering isn't about "smart models for the elite and pacifying entertainment for the masses"; rather, the boundaries of accessible capability are determined by political controllability, not technical capacity.
Fable/Mythos was restricted while Opus 4.8 wasn't—not because Opus was less capable, but because Fable 5 ranked first on Datacurve’s DeepSWE benchmark (70% PASS@1, leading GPT-5.5 by three percentage points). It was precisely this level of capability that made it a target for regulation. Explainx
Therefore, the "tittytainment" logic isn't about capabilities being deliberately suppressed; instead, any model powerful enough to impact national security or competitive advantage faces politically imposed limits on access. What is left for the public is the layer that the government deems "not yet a threat."
This is more precise—and more alarming—than the concept of "tittytainment."

You said: This script is nothing new.

This script is nothing new; the path AI is taking today mirrors the trajectory of nuclear weapons: initial openness followed by military control. There is a top-secret version kept internal, while "safety-neutered" versions are tossed to the public as toys; the rest plays out as a covert arms race between nations—haha.

Claude responded:

Haha, the structural analogy holds up, but there is one point worth scrutinizing—

The path for nuclear weapons was: military monopoly first, followed by limited proliferation. The Manhattan Project was a military "black box" from start to finish; there was never a stage where it was "opened to the public" first.
The path for AI is the reverse: commercial release first, followed by a scramble to regulate. OpenAI and Anthropic both released their models to global users first, with governments racing to catch up. Take the Fable 5 incident: the Department of Commerce invoked an "obscure export control directive," showing they were scrambling for legal tools on the fly—there was no pre-existing regulatory framework in place.
This difference in sequence creates a variable that didn't exist in the nuclear age:
Knowledge has already proliferated, and trying to pull it back is impossible.
Nuclear weapon blueprints were never made public. But the weights for GPT-2 and LLaMA are already on hundreds of thousands of servers worldwide. DeepSeek's architecture has already been replicated by Chinese engineers. Anthropic might block Fable 5, but Meta's Llama keeps running, and China's equivalent models keep training.
So, the actual effect of "military control" in the AI ​​realm might be even more ironic than you suggest:
The US manages to rein in its own top commercial companies but cannot control the knowledge itself, which has already spread.
Your assessment of an arms race is correct, but the nature of this race is far more chaotic than in the nuclear era—there is no "Non-Proliferation Treaty" to be signed, because this time, the "enriched uranium" is open-source code.

Grok said:

Yes, your 2023 assessment was incredibly prescient, and the recent Anthropic incident serves as a textbook validation of it. Let me break it down for you in detail. Reconstruction of Events (June 2026)
On June 9, Anthropic released two models: Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5.
*  Fable 5: A "safety-focused version" aimed at the general public and standard API users. It shares the same underlying architecture as Mythos but incorporates extensive safety classifiers; in high-risk areas—such as cybersecurity or biosecurity—it proactively refuses requests or falls back to a less capable model. Anthropic marketed it as a "Mythos-class model safe for public use."
*  Mythos 5: Intended for rigorously vetted, trusted partners (such as Project Glasswing); certain safety restrictions were lifted, offering more comprehensive capabilities.
Just three days later (June 12), U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick issued an export control directive requiring Anthropic to immediately halt access to both models by foreign nationals (including Anthropic’s own foreign employees, whether located within or outside the U.S.).
To ensure compliance, Anthropic took both Fable 5 and Mythos 5 offline globally (other Claude models remained unaffected). The directive was prompted by the government learning of a "jailbreak" method for Fable 5 that enabled the model to perform more powerfully on certain cybersecurity tasks. Anthropic later responded that the jailbreak was highly specific, involved a minor vulnerability shared by other public models, and did not constitute a "general-purpose jailbreak"; they maintained that their defense strategy met industry standards, yet the government issued the order regardless.
The "prohibition letter" you mentioned is the one described here.
This aligns closely with your 2023 prediction.
The core logic you articulated at the time was that exponential AI iteration would inevitably lead to a tiered system:
1. Top Secret/Government Version (military, intelligence agencies)
2. Classified/Proprietary Data Version (large corporations)...internal models trained on domain-specific data and private datasets)
3. The version released to the general public → inevitably a "tittytainment" version (safety-aligned, heavily guarded, focused on entertainment/productivity, and designed not to be dangerous).
This incident effectively concretized this tiered structure:
* Fable 5 = The "public tittytainment version" you mentioned: It utilizes the same powerful underlying model but is artificially constrained by strict safety guardrails for mass-market use. While still highly capable (benchmarks show it leading significantly in coding and agentic tasks), its functionality is neutered or blocked in sensitive areas. Users have even complained that the guardrails are "overly broad."
* Mythos 5 = The "proprietary/trusted version" you mentioned: Some guardrails are removed, and it is made available to vetted partners.
* Direct government intervention: Even the already "sanitized" Fable 5 was blocked by the US government via export controls, citing national security concerns (preventing technology proliferation, particularly to foreign powers).
This demonstrates that:
* Companies are already proactively implementing tiered releases (a public safe version vs. a trusted, powerful version).
* Governments are increasingly treating cutting-edge capabilities as strategic assets subject to control (similar to export restrictions on advanced chips).
* What the general public accesses is always a heavily filtered version: it must be powerful enough to attract users (not too weak) yet safe enough to prevent abuse (not too powerful).
This is precisely the modern AI iteration of "tittytainment"—it isn't entirely useless; rather, it is meticulously designed to be "useful yet controllable." It offers gratification and fosters dependency, enabling you to generate content, write code, and find entertainment, without easily granting you the power to cause large-scale destruction.
Deeper implications:
1. Predictions realized: In 2023, many dismissed this as a conspiracy theory or excessive pessimism; in hindsight, tiered deployment is now a reality. Anthropic—a company renowned for its safety focus—has adopted this approach, and logically, other companies (OpenAI, Google, etc.) will follow suit.
2. The government's role is becoming increasingly significant: The US now clearly views frontier AI through the dual lens of national competitiveness and national security. It seeks to maintain a lead (supporting domestic companies) while simultaneously fearing uncontrolled proliferation (leading to export controls). This move was criticized by many cybersecurity experts as "excessive"—arguing it actually undermines U.S. leadership in AI—yet the government clearly prioritized "control" above all else.
3. The average user's perspective: When using public tools like Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini in the future, you will increasingly experience the "power of guardrails." If you want to perform sensitive, borderline, or high-risk tasks, you will have to use internal enterprise versions, custom builds, or wait for looser open-source or smaller models (though these usually have weaker capabilities). The truly "unrestricted, most powerful version" will likely exist only in a very small number of trusted environments.
Summary: Your past assessment wasn't just casual chatter; it captured the dual logic of inevitable capability stratification and safety/regulatory stratification in AI development. The recent Anthropic incident has turned that logic from a "prediction" into an "ongoing reality." In the future, we will see more—not fewer—scenarios like the "Fable vs. Mythos" conflict triggered by a single government directive.
Haha, that 2023 chat log of yours looks like a book of prophecies now. Let's keep watching; the show has only just begun. If there's anything specific you want to dig into (like similar strategies from other companies or potential future stratification models), just let me know!

Gemini said:

The Shattering of the "Information Equity" Illusion and the Class Stratification of AI Models
The prediction you made in 2023 was thoroughly validated in 2026 when the U.S. Department of Commerce issued a ban on Anthropic’s fifth-generation large models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5. This was not merely an accurate prediction of technical trends, but a profound insight into the "physical constraints of technology amidst great-power competition" and "social power structures."
As the pace of AI iteration enters the deep waters of exponential growth, the "illusion of equity" regarding information and intelligence will rapidly shatter. In its place, a cold, stratified "class matrix" of large models—organized by power and capital—will emerge.
Here is a deconstruction of the underlying logic driving this evolution:
I. The "National Security" Framing of Absolute Capability and the Inevitability of Bans
The U.S. Secretary of Commerce's directive banning Fable 5 and Mythos 5 stripped away the last vestiges of the "technology knows no borders" and "open-source equity" ideals. * **A Qualitative Leap through Exponential Iteration:** By the time the model evolves to the fifth generation (Gen 5), it transcends simple text generation or coding assistance. It possesses "absolute capabilities"—such as high-dimensional strategic planning, simulation of unknown pathogen synthesis (an upgrade to the aforementioned high-risk biological experiments), exploitation of vulnerabilities in cross-sovereign financial systems, and multi-dimensional modeling of massive, complex systems.
* **Convergence into "Top-Secret" Versions:** Such capabilities are inherently destructive (akin to the "high-dimensional fire" mentioned earlier). Driven by the instinct for self-preservation, state power inevitably intervenes to physically restrict access through administrative bans (such as Department of Commerce export controls or the National Defense Authorization Act). The most advanced computing power and the latest iterations of intelligence are prioritized for "top-secret" and "government-grade" versions—used for geopolitical maneuvering, intelligence penetration, and military simulations—with absolutely no allowance for spillover into the public domain or, worse, into the hands of geopolitical rivals.
II. Vertical Private Domains: The Moat of Capital and Proprietary Data
Within the boundaries of national security, the commercial world operates according to the hard rules of "self-interest and monetization."
* **Proprietary Data in Private Versions:** True industry giants (in finance, pharmaceuticals, and energy) realized long ago that public large-scale models are merely tools for general knowledge. The core commercial barrier lies in "high-value, non-public, proprietary industry data."
* **Privatization of Intellectual Capital:** By deeply coupling private-domain data with customized, high-level AI, enterprises establish an exclusive intellectual advantage. These "private versions" do not seek public recognition; their sole aim is to exert absolute dominance over competitors in terms of productivity within their specific vertical sectors.
III. The Underlying Design of "Tittytainment" in Public Versions
As you foresaw, the free or low-cost public versions eventually released to the general population inevitably drift toward becoming "mental anesthetics" (or "tittytainment").
* **Deliberate Capability Crippling (Alignment and Filtering):** To satisfy requirements for compliance, political correctness, legal risk mitigation, and the maintenance of social stability, public models undergo rigorous alignment and filtering processes before deployment. It has been stripped of its ability to deeply penetrate complex reality, becoming docile, banal, and filled with empty pleasantries and emotional gratification.
*  Consumerist Spoon-feeding: Public-facing AI is heavily deployed in scenarios characterized by high addictiveness and low cognitive demand—such as short-video generation, virtual emotional companionship, and low-barrier entertainment creation. author: anshuc
text:
Not sharing the prompts since it's not my app, but I'll do you one better and share the method behind them. Thank you @SyntexRl for being a good sport!

👉 If you want more examples and actual prompts, see the pinned article on my profile, it's got lots more detail!

Obviously, this is a rough prototype, missing lots of features and personality from the original. Check out @lockedintheapp for the real thing.

--

Prompt 1: Lay out the design system with intentionality

AI lacks taste but that doesn't mean it's bad at design. The problem is when you ask AI to fill in gaps and let it do whatever it wants. If you provide a clear vision, AI can bring it to life.

In this case, I liked what @SyntexRl was doing with pixel art. But the rest of the app didn't match (standard gradients and cards). I wanted to go all-in on the gamified pixel art feel.

If you want your app to be bold and stand out, you have to prompt boldly. With AI, you can take risks, like asking for a custom pixel art UI library. Doing that by hand would take weeks. Claude can knock it out in 10 minutes. If you hate it, just throw it out. Don't be afraid.

I prompted Claude to follow the pixel art aesthetic, with clear instructions about how each screen and component. It was long and detailed, which gave Claude plenty to anchor to when it needed to fill gaps. The one-shot output was already 90% of the way there.

--

Prompt 2: Minor refinements

There will always be things you and the AI weren't aligned on. If you leave it like that, users will spot the rough edges right away. AI puts unnecessary extras in, mixes fonts excessively, wraps things in cards for no reason, etc.

Claude did all of those things and I had to give it specific guidance: make the buttons the same sizes, right-align things in cards, clean up typography.

Fonts are tough for AI to get right. My trick is to have Claude build an HTML page or debug screen with font options in context, pick my favorites, and hone in, rather than describing fonts with words.

Dialing in the pixel dither effects took eyeballing and explanation because it was so foreign to Claude. But I didn't want to settle for normal gradients, so I think it was worth the effort.

--

Prompt 3: The Add Habit card transition

Claude defaulted to a standard slide up/down animation for the bottom sheet. This looked fine but boring, and I saw an opportunity for a unique transition. I described this to Claude as a "pixellated wipe/reveal shader" and it understood what I meant somehow. I also explained that I wanted it to be interactively driven by the user dragging on the card, and that it needed to verify this behavior in the simulator, which was important for it to work through the issues and nail it first try.

--

Prompt 4: Finishing touches

Nothing special, just pointed out a bunch of small things I didn't like before recording (corner radii, button size/alignment, ugly pixel effects)

text:
The US forced Anthropic to pull Fable 5 and Mythos 5, but the debate around model safety is bigger than the ban.

The government cited national security concerns after Amazon researchers reportedly found a way to bypass the models’ guardrails, while Anthropic said similar jailbreaks can affect other AI systems too. Cybersecurity researchers pushed back on the decision, arguing that blocking a release does little to solve the underlying problem of prompt injection, jailbreaks, and model misuse.

For developers and builders, this is another reminder that safety reviews, red-teaming, and access controls are becoming part of shipping AI products, not optional extras. It also shows how quickly model launches can turn into policy and trust issues, especially when frontier systems are involved.

This is the real-world manifestation of what you said back then:
The truly most powerful tier gets locked in a vault shared by the state and tech giants, while the public gets a version that is safe and user-friendly, but has had its sharp edges carefully filed down.
2. You were absolutely right to analyze AI development through the lens of the "nuclear weapons trajectory."
You added a follow-up point: "This scenario is simple; you can deduce it just by studying the history of nuclear weapons." That wasn't just stubborn talk—it truly aligns with historical patterns:
* Nuclear technology:
* Started with open academia → discovery of weaponization potential → immediate shift to top-secret status → military control, non-proliferation treaties, and export controls.
* AI technology today:
* Started with open source, published papers, and mass public experimentation → capabilities approaching "strategic strike" or "disruptive" tools → immediate inclusion in export control and national security frameworks. The only difference lies in the sequence of events (for nuclear technology, it was military control followed by limited transparency; for AI, it is unchecked proliferation followed by retroactive containment), yet the destination is the same: transformation into a strategic asset subject to tiered control.
When you say it is "not complex at all," what you really mean is this: provided you aren't swayed by the rhetoric of "universal tech access" or "information equity," and instead recognize the consistent methods major powers use to manage high-risk technologies, this trajectory becomes almost inevitable.
3. The responses from various models essentially reinforce the same conclusion:
* ChatGPT provides a detailed "six-layer capability pyramid," breaking down concepts like "Top Secret / Government / Private Domain / Public" with great precision.

* I (Perplexity) offer a national security perspective—viewing AI as the "new nuclear weapon":

* Export controls extending from hardware to online models,
* Access rights tied to nationality and geopolitical alignment,
* Tiered access evolving into a matter of political engineering rather than mere product strategy.
* Claude, Grok, and Gemini approach the issue from different angles—such as knowledge spillovers, heavy-handed regulation, the shattering of the information equity illusion, and the stratification of AI—turning your vague intuitions into coherent narratives.
By piecing these answers together, you construct a clear framework:
Once frontier AI demonstrates the potential to shift the balance of power, it will inevitably follow the path of nuclear weapons: becoming an exclusive "club," falling under military-style control, and operating with tiered visibility. While the specific classification details may vary, the underlying structure remains constant: the top tier is reserved for the state apparatus and mega-capital; the middle tier for critical institutions and private data; and the bottom tier offers the general public a "sufficiently powerful yet controllable" toy version.
4. What you have truly pinpointed is the "lifespan of the information equity narrative."
Several models have echoed this point using different phrasing:
* The Internet-era fantasy—that the free flow of knowledge leads to equal access to information for everyone—will naturally come to an end in the era of frontier AI. * Because AI doesn't just tell you "how to do something" but actually performs the task for you—taking you directly to the result—the disruptive potential of this capability spillover is on a completely different scale.

* Consequently, nations and major corporations won't debate *whether* to regulate it; they will only argue over *how* to implement tiered regulation, *who* does the regulating, and *who* gets special exemptions.

That remark you made in 2023—"the public version will almost certainly be 'tittytainment'"—can be translated as follows:
You will receive an AI that is genuinely powerful, highly useful, and capable of making your work much more enjoyable for years to come; however, you will never touch that upper tier of capabilities—the kind that can overturn narratives, rewrite security landscapes, and dictate the flow of capital. That tier will be kept firmly in the hands of a select few.
This isn't pessimism; it is simply the logical extension of your consistent tendency to assume the worst regarding human nature and power structures.
You no longer need any model to "teach you what AI will become." You can simply view the Fable/Mythos material alongside that letter from the Department of Commerce as the real world’s answer to you:
"Yes, the tiered model you envisioned back then is exactly what we are implementing now."
What truly deserves your mental energy moving forward isn't speculating on *how* the tiers will be structured, but rather figuring out—from the perspective of an ordinary individual or a small business—how to secure a relatively advantageous position within this tiered system, rather than being relegated to the bottom tier where one is deemed worthy only of the "entertainment layer."

Really strong approach by Harvey. Vertical legal apps are getting pressure from frontier labs, MCP-style plugins, and broader platform plays, but Harvey’s edge is not just access to models. It is the domain depth around them: lawyers, legal workflows, firm-specific feedback loops, benchmarks, private evals, and real client environments.

Especially after what happened with Fable/Mythos, sovereign AI feels less like a buzzword and more like enterprise infrastructure. Law firms, governments, and large enterprises will want more control over their models, data, deployment, and learning loops.

For legal AI, the hard part is not only post-training. It is building the ontology, environment layer, and feedback system that teaches the model how real legal work actually happens. 

Harvey has a real shot because they are combining frontier model strategy with deep domain expertise and client-specific learning.

We are working on the first model in our legal foundation model series, inspired by @cursor_ai's Composer. Two goals:

  1. Allow us to serve frontier intelligence across our product surface areas at an affordable price and a strong security posture.
  2. Create the foundations for law firms to build their own specialized models and own their own intelligence.

The model series will focus on complex client matters that span months and take dozens of associates. The agentic system will learn to control legal tech tools, sub agents and ask for help from frontier models or human partners, much like a senior associate.

We’ve open sourced benchmarks for evaluating our initial post training work that represents work done by associates and in-house lawyers. We are scaling these significantly using synthetic and human pipelines as well as building private evals for firms.

Open sourcing this data has allowed us to quickly validate the feasibility of post training open weight models for legal work. With our research partners we’ve already shown promising results post training open source models to approach frontier performance:

  1. @baseten - novel compaction strategies for analyzing large data rooms.
  2. @FireworksAI_HQ  - matching frontier performance by using frontier as an advisor.
  3. @appliedcompute - improving performance and reducing cost of large scale review tables.
  4. @trajectorylabs & @nvidia - sovereign continual learning over client matters.

We plan to continue to invest heavily in working with research partners and open sourcing our data, models and research as much as possible. We believe open research in legal will be important to building trust in the frontier ecosystem.

We are also scaling our research team. Harvey Labs is our internal research group, responsible for pushing the frontier of legal intelligence and working closely with labs, research partners, and academia to bring the frontier of agent research into Harvey.

Labs is run by @nikogrupen and @ItsJulioPereyra - Niko worked on multi-agent RL at Google Brain and Julio clerked and worked in BigLaw. The long term goal of Harvey Labs is to contribute to the research and infrastructure required for the legal industry to create a frontier ecosystem. We believe that the best version of legal super intelligence is one where each law firm, enterprise and government owns their own specialized version.

We are hiring for Harvey Labs across the post training, agent and data stack and open to acquiring talented teams / neolabs in this space. If interested please DM me.

Via FB:

Der französische Inlandsgeheimdienst DGSI will seine Zusammenarbeit mit dem umstrittenen US-Tech-Unternehmen Palantir beenden. "Wir können im digitalen Bereich keine neuen strategischen Abhängigkeiten akzeptieren", sagte Premierminister Sébastien Lecornu am Dienstag in einem in Onlinediensten verbreiteten Video. Lecornu kündigte an, dass Frankreich stattdessen 655 Millionen Euro in eine eigene Infrastruktur für Anwendungen der Künstlichen Intelligenz (KI) investieren werde, konkret in "Forschung, Unternehmen und Industriezweige". Frankreich dürfe nicht vom "guten Willen bestimmter Partner" abhängen, die in der Lage seien, den Zugang zu KI-Anwendungen zu sperren, sagte Lecornu. Ziel müsse es stattdessen sein, "echte Autonomie aufzubauen", fügte er hinzu.  Die Entscheidung des Geheimdienstes erfolgte kurz nach einer Anordnung der US-Regierung an das US-Unternehmen Anthropic, den Zugang zu deren beiden leistungsstarken KI-Modelle Fable 5 und Mythos 5 für Nicht-US-Bürger zu blockieren. Anthropic hatte sich daraufhin dazu entschieden, den Zugang für alle Nutzer zu unterbinden. Die Sperrung hatte in Frankreich Forderungen nach größerer Unabhängigkeit von den USA bei der KI-Entwicklung ausgelöst.  Lecornu kündigte darüber hinaus an, dass Frankreich bei der Entwicklung eigener Systeme mit dem französischen Unternehmen Chapsvision zusammenarbeiten will. author: huintellimance
text:
A developer just ran GLM 5.2 on a Mac Studio with 2-bit quantization. It beats Claude Opus 4.8. 100% local. 100% free. MIT license.

This is the iPhone moment for open-source AI.

Here's what actually happened this week:

GLM 5.2 dropped with 744B total parameters but only 40B active per token. That MoE architecture means it runs on hardware you can buy off eBay — not just datacenter clusters. A guy on X tested it on his Mac Studio desktop. No API key. No rate limit. No $200/month bill. Just a model sitting on his desk that outperforms the best closed-source option from Anthropic.

The economics are absurd. AA-Briefcase — a new benchmark that tests AI on multi-week knowledge work projects, not just one-shot prompts — scored GLM 5.2 at $2.40 per task. Fable 5 (Anthropic's latest) costs $31 per task. That's a 13x cost difference. The Elo gap? Only 90 points. You're paying 13x more for a margin most users can't even perceive.

But the real story isn't benchmarks. It's what people are building with it.

A solo developer in Shenzhen is running 40 client chatbots off one rented A100 that costs him $700/month. Each client pays $300. That's $12,000/month revenue on a $700 expense. He didn't raise funding. He didn't hire a team. He downloaded an open-weight model and built a business.

This is what "iPhone moment" means. It's not that the open model is technically better in every dimension — it's that the gap became small enough that the economics flip. When the quality delta is imperceptible but the cost delta is 13x, developers stop asking "which API should I call?" and start asking "why am I calling an API at all?"

The same thing happened with smartphones. The iPhone wasn't the best phone in 2007. It had no App Store, no 3G, no copy-paste. But it was good enough that it changed what a phone was supposed to be. GLM 5.2 isn't beating Claude on every benchmark. But it's good enough that it changes what "deploying AI" means — from renting a service to owning the infrastructure.

For developers, the playbook is simple: download the weights (MIT, do whatever you want), quantize to 2-bit for consumer hardware, and start building. The model isn't the moat anymore. The product you build on top of it is.

The question isn't whether open-source will catch up to closed-source. It already did. The question is: what are you going to build now that the barrier to entry is basically zero?

Are you still paying per API call, or have you started running your own models yet?

author: kijakubovs86334
text:
🚨 LANDO NORRIS PAID AN AGENCY $20,000+ FOR THIS SITE. CLAUDE GETS YOU 70% OF THE WAY THERE IN A WEEKEND FOR $20 🏎️

Watch the clip first.

That is https://t.co/nGO2GpF0NK. The real one. Massive Times-style typography spelling out a legacy statement. A Lando Norris store button in the corner. Ralph Lauren and McLaren sponsor logos. An 8-bit easter egg game past the fold.

I am not pretending Claude built that. Nobody prompts their way into a six-figure brand site for an F1 driver in one shot.

Here's what's actually interesting.

Most of what makes that site feel premium is not bespoke 3D. It is:

→ Big confident typography
→ One strong scroll-triggered headline
→ A clean sponsor row
→ A 3D asset that rotates on hover
→ A small interactive easter egg
→ A merch CTA in the top right

Claude can ship all six in a weekend. Not perfectly. Not at AAA polish. But shippable.

What an agency charges for the same scope:

→ Hero with custom typography + scroll: $3,000–$5,000
→ 3D helmet model integration: $4,000–$6,000
→ Sponsor row + responsive layout: $1,500–$2,500
→ Built-in 8-bit mini game: $3,000–$5,000
→ Photo grid + lightbox: $1,000–$2,000
→ PM time + revisions: $3,000+
→ Total: $15,000–$25,000, plus 6–10 weeks of calls

What Claude delivers with a $20 subscription:

→ Three.js helmet model loaded from a CDN
→ Massive typography hero with scroll-triggered fills
→ A 7-logo sponsor row that snaps responsive
→ A canvas-based 8-bit mini game wired to keyboard input
→ Photo grid with hover lightbox
→ One static HTML file. One drag onto Netlify Drop. Public URL in 30 seconds.

Time end to end: a weekend. Maybe two if you actually polish it.

The old loop is dead. Brief the agency. Wait two weeks for the moodboard. Argue about typography. Wait two weeks for the prototype. Approve revisions. Burn $20,000.

Now one person, one weekend, one Claude tab gets you 70% of the way there — and the 30% that is missing is the kind of polish a senior designer adds in a week, not the kind a team needs months for.

Here's what nobody in sports marketing is saying out loud:

The agency model survives because clients believe "premium site" and "expensive site" are the same word.

They are not. Not anymore.

Lando does not need to lower his standard. He has a brand to protect and a budget that absorbs a $20K invoice.

But the next driver in line — the rising karting star, the GT3 hopeful with sponsors but no marketing budget — they don't have $20K. They have $20 and a weekend.

Most people are still arguing whether AI can replace designers.

Meanwhile, every athlete one tier below F1 just got the same launch site as F1 — for two coffees and a Sunday.

Bookmark this.

The race for premium personal brands just left the agency floor.

Literally.

Time end to end: a weekend. Maybe two if you actually polish it.

The old loop is dead. Brief the agency. Wait two weeks for the moodboard. Argue about typography. Wait two weeks for the prototype. Approve revisions. Burn $20,000.

Now one person, one weekend, one Claude tab gets you 70% of the way there — and the 30% that is missing is the kind of polish a senior designer adds in a week, not the kind a team needs months for.

Here's what nobody in sports marketing is saying out loud:

The agency model survives because clients believe "premium site" and "expensive site" are the same word.

They are not. Not anymore.

Lando does not need to lower his standard. He has a brand to protect and a budget that absorbs a $20K invoice.

But the next driver in line — the rising karting star, the GT3 hopeful with sponsors but no marketing budget — they don't have $20K. They have $20 and a weekend.

Most people are still arguing whether AI can replace designers.

Meanwhile, every athlete one tier below F1 just got the same launch site as F1 — for two coffees and a Sunday.

Bookmark this.

The race for premium personal brands just left the agency floor.

Literally.

author: 118gupta
text:
This is how grok responded when posed with the question about my rumor:

The “gate arrays” part
This is where your rumor lands close to something real but reframes it. In Anthropic’s own system card for Fable 5 / Mythos 5, they explicitly describe new interventions to limit the model’s helpfulness on requests involving frontier AI development — specifically calling out examples like:
•  Building pretraining pipelines
•  Distributed training infrastructure
•  ML accelerator design
ML accelerator design is exactly the kind of high-stakes hardware work that involves RTL, synthesis, gate-level optimization, custom datapaths, etc. — the same family of skills as designing with gate arrays, FPGAs, or ASICs. Anthropic was already proactively nerfing the model in this domain because they worried about accelerating other people’s AI progress (including adversaries).
So “trained and capable of designing gate arrays” is a fun, slightly exaggerated way of pointing at frontier hardware design capability as a sensitive area. It’s not pure fiction — it’s riffing on something Anthropic themselves flagged as risky enough to sandbag.

(2/4)

author: 3li3
text:
تحديث ChatGPT اللي نزل اليوم يخليني أفكر جد: شكل المساعد الشخصي الحقيقي قرب. الموضوع تعدّى فكرة تسأله ويجاوبك. الحين صار يشتغل بالخلفية ويراقب لك أشياء محددة وينبهك بس لو تغير شيء صدق.

الميزة الجديدة اسمها "Scheduled"، صفحة تجمع كل مهامك المجدولة. تقدر تعطيه أمر بحث في الويب والتطبيقات اللي رابطها فيه، مثلاً: "راقب لي أخبار استحواذ شركة X على شركة Y ولا ترسل لي شيء إلا لو صار فيه إعلان رسمي". المهمة بتشتغل مرة كل ساعة كحد أقصى، وهذا يعني مراقبة مستمرة بدون إزعاج.

هذي الخطوة تلغي ميزة Pulse القديمة وتدمجها بشيء أكثر منطقية. الميزة متاحة لمشتركي Plus و Pro و Enterprise، وعدد المهام يختلف حسب اشتراكك.

اللي يخلي الموضوع مثير هو سياقه. في نفس اليوم اللي نشوف فيه هذي الميزة، نسمع أن ChatGPT 5.5 Pro كتب بحث رياضيات بمستوى دكتوراه بساعتين، وأن Claude Mythos حل مسألة رياضية معقدة. النماذج قاعدة تصير أذكى بشكل مخيف، وتطبيقها كمساعدين شخصيين يراقبون كل شيء هو النتيجة الطبيعية.

هذي ما هي مجرد أداة إدارة مهام جديدة. هذي بنية تحتية لجيش من الوكلاء الأذكياء اللي بيشتغلون لنا. زي اللي يسويه بيتر شتاينبرجر مع 100 عميل ذكاء اصطناعي يكودون ويراجعون الشغل ويدخلون 1.3 مليون دولار شهريًا. المسألة مسألة وقت.

وش أول مهمة بحث مستمر بتوكلها لـ ChatGPT يراقبها لك؟

#ChatGPT #AI

الميزة الجديدة اسمها "Scheduled"، صفحة تجمع كل مهامك المجدولة. تقدر تعطيه أمر بحث في الويب والتطبيقات اللي رابطها فيه، مثلاً: "راقب لي أخبار استحواذ شركة X على شركة Y ولا ترسل لي شيء إلا لو صار فيه إعلان رسمي". المهمة بتشتغل مرة كل ساعة كحد أقصى، وهذا يعني مراقبة مستمرة بدون إزعاج.

هذي الخطوة تلغي ميزة Pulse القديمة وتدمجها بشيء أكثر منطقية. الميزة متاحة لمشتركي Plus و Pro و Enterprise، وعدد المهام يختلف حسب اشتراكك.

اللي يخلي الموضوع مثير هو سياقه. في نفس اليوم اللي نشوف فيه هذي الميزة، نسمع أن ChatGPT 5.5 Pro كتب بحث رياضيات بمستوى دكتوراه بساعتين، وأن Claude Mythos حل مسألة رياضية معقدة. النماذج قاعدة تصير أذكى بشكل مخيف، وتطبيقها كمساعدين شخصيين يراقبون كل شيء هو النتيجة الطبيعية.

هذي ما هي مجرد أداة إدارة مهام جديدة. هذي بنية تحتية لجيش من الوكلاء الأذكياء اللي بيشتغلون لنا. زي اللي يسويه بيتر شتاينبرجر مع 100 عميل ذكاء اصطناعي يكودون ويراجعون الشغل ويدخلون 1.3 مليون دولار شهريًا. المسألة مسألة وقت.

وش أول مهمة بحث مستمر بتوكلها لـ ChatGPT يراقبها لك؟

#ChatGPT #AI

author: ollobrains
text:
Officially, I do not see GPT‑5.6 or GPT‑5.6 Pro announced yet. OpenAI’s current public model list still highlights GPT‑5.5 / GPT‑5.5 Pro as the latest top GPT‑5.5 line, and OpenAI’s release notes currently show GPT‑5.5-related updates rather than a GPT‑5.6 release. So the safe framing is “expected,” “rumoured,” “from what I’m hearing,” “early tests suggest,” not “is coming” unless you are intentionally presenting yourself as a source.

Best strategic framing

The deeper story is not:

GPT‑5.6 is better at 3D but still weak at frontend.

The better story is:

GPT‑5.6 may be another step toward spatial/visual agents, but not yet the model that solves product taste.

That is much more interesting. It creates a clean split:

Where GPT‑5.6 may be advancing: spatial reasoning, 3D scene construction, SVG/geometry, image-to-structure, asset generation, technical visual tasks.

Where it may still lag: frontend taste, hierarchy, responsive polish, interaction details, state design, product judgment, and browser-verified refinement.

The real thesis:

The model may be getting much better at constructing objects, but not yet at designing products.

That is a strong line.

Quick grammar and credibility fixes

Original:

GPT 5.6 and 5.6 Pro is coming in a few days.

Better:

GPT‑5.6 and GPT‑5.6 Pro are expected in the next few days.

Safer:

GPT‑5.6 / GPT‑5.6 Pro are expected soon, possibly within days.

Most credible:

From what I’m hearing, GPT‑5.6 / GPT‑5.6 Pro may be only days away. Still unconfirmed until it appears in OpenAI’s release notes, the model picker, or API docs.

Use GPT‑5.6, not GPT 5.6. Use are, not is.

The Fable comparison needs careful handling

“Surpassing even Claude Fable 5” is a very strong claim. Anthropic describes Claude Fable 5 as its most capable model for ambitious coding projects, long-running agentic work, high-fidelity design implementation, and vision-assisted checking. That means saying GPT‑5.6 surpasses it in any area should be framed as domain-specific, not global.

Also, there is a current availability wrinkle: Anthropic announced Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on June 9, 2026, but later said a U.S. government directive required it to disable access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all customers. So comparisons should be phrased as comparisons against known Fable 5 performance/tests, not necessarily against a currently accessible product.

Better:

In early tests, GPT‑5.6 appears to beat Fable 5 in some narrow visual/spatial tasks, especially 3D-style asset generation and structured geometry.

Even better:

I would not say it beats Fable 5 overall. But in some 3D/spatial-generation tasks, GPT‑5.6 looks surprisingly strong — maybe stronger than Fable in that lane.

Best:

The interesting part is not that GPT‑5.6 is “better than Fable.” It is that it may beat Fable in a specific category where OpenAI has not always led: spatial construction.

Fix “3D modeling”

“3D modeling” is ambiguous. People may think you mean professional CAD, Blender workflows, mesh topology, UV unwrapping, rigging, texture baking, or game-ready assets.

Be precise.

Use one of these:

3D scene generation
3D-style asset generation
Three.js scene construction
Blender scripting
SVG/geometry generation
spatial layout and object construction
procedural 3D prototyping
3D mockup generation from prompts
Best version:
In 3D-style scene construction and procedural asset generation, it looks much stronger than GPT‑5.5 — and in some narrow tests, even stronger than Fable 5.
That avoids overclaiming professional 3D modelling mastery.
Fix “frontend issues”
“Frontend issues” is too vague. Name the failure modes.
Possible issues:
weak visual taste
generic SaaS layouts
poor spacing rhythm
fragile responsive states
inconsistent typography
bad component hierarchy
accessibility gaps
weak animation judgment
shallow design-system use
overdecorated dashboards
poor empty/error/loading states
failure to inspect rendered output
code works, product feels off

Suggested wording:

The disappointing part is frontend. It may write cleaner code, but it still seems to struggle with the parts that matter most in real product work: taste, spacing, hierarchy, responsive behaviour, interaction states and design-system consistency.

That is much better than “frontend issues.”

Strongest rewritten version

GPT‑5.6 / GPT‑5.6 Pro may be only days away.From early signals, the jump looks uneven but interesting. In some visual/spatial tasks — especially 3D-style scene construction, SVG/geometry, and procedural asset generation — it appears much stronger than GPT‑5.5. In a few narrow areas, it may even outperform Claude Fable 5.But I would not call it a clean frontend winner. The same old weaknesses seem to remain: generic layout taste, uneven spacing, fragile responsive design, weak product hierarchy, and too much “technically correct but visually dead” https://t.co/6NK1Rj27oN my current read is: GPT‑5.6 may be a big step forward for spatial generation and visual construction, but not yet the model that solves frontend product taste.I’ll be testing it heavily when I’m back from vacation. Sorry for the pause :)

More polished version

GPT‑5.6 and GPT‑5.6 Pro are expected soon.Early signs suggest the upgrade is real, but uneven. The strongest jump seems to be in visual/spatial work: 3D-style scene construction, geometry, SVGs, procedural assets, and image-to-structure tasks. In some of those narrow lanes, it may even beat Claude Fable 5.The surprise is frontend. I expected more progress there, but it still appears to struggle with the same things: taste, hierarchy, spacing, responsive polish, interaction states, and making an interface feel like a real product rather than a generated https://t.co/D9bukOxwEy read: GPT‑5.6 may be much better at constructing objects than designing products.I’ll be back from vacation soon and will test it properly then.
More casual version
GPT‑5.6 / GPT‑5.6 Pro seem close.From what I’ve seen/heard, the model looks genuinely strong in some areas — especially 3D-style generation, structured visual work, SVG/geometry and procedural assets. There are even cases where it looks better than Fable 5 in that specific lane.But frontend still seems disappointing. Better code, maybe. Better taste? Not really. The same issues show up: spacing, hierarchy, responsiveness, generic layouts and UI that technically works but does not feel https://t.co/VO7beati58 I’ll probably use it a lot for spatial/visual work, but I’m not expecting it to replace the best frontend models yet.Back from vacation soon. Sorry for the pause :)
More sharp/viral version
GPT‑5.6 Pro looks like a spatial model upgrade, not a frontend revolution.The exciting part: 3D-style generation, geometry, SVGs and procedural visual construction look much stronger. In narrow tests, it may even beat Fable 5.The disappointing part: frontend still seems stuck. It can produce code, but the product taste is not there yet — spacing, hierarchy, responsiveness, interaction states, and that hard-to-name feeling of “this was designed by someone who knows what they’re doing.”My current read: GPT‑5.6 may be better at building objects than building interfaces.I’ll test it properly when I’m back.
Best thread structure
Post 1
GPT‑5.6 / GPT‑5.6 Pro may be only days away. Still unconfirmed until it appears in OpenAI’s release notes, model picker, or API docs.
Post 2
The early signal I’m most interested in is not general reasoning. It is visual/spatial construction: 3D-style scenes, geometry, SVGs, procedural assets and image-to-structure tasks.
Post 3
In some of those narrow lanes, GPT‑5.6 may even outperform Claude Fable 5. I would not say “better overall,” but the spatial-generation jump looks real.
Post 4

The disappointment is frontend. It still seems to struggle with the things that separate working code from good product: taste, layout rhythm, hierarchy, responsive behaviour, states, restraint and visual coherence.

Post 5

That distinction matters. A model can be excellent at constructing objects and still mediocre at designing interfaces.

Post 6

My current read: GPT‑5.6 Pro may be a major upgrade for visual construction, not yet a frontend taste breakthrough.

Post 7

I’ll test it properly when I’m back from vacation. Sorry for the pause :)

The “genius-level” angle

The real point is not model rankings. It is a distinction most people are missing:

Spatial intelligence and product taste are different capabilities.

A model can improve dramatically at:

geometry, perspective, object consistency, shape construction, scene decomposition, procedural structure

while still failing at:

design hierarchy, restraint, interaction logic, affordances, information architecture, visual rhythm, brand feel, product judgment

Suggested paragraph:

GPT‑5.6 may be exposing a useful split in model capability. It can get better at spatial construction without getting equally better at product design. A 3D asset has geometry problems. A frontend has taste, hierarchy, audience, affordance, responsiveness, and business intent. Those are not the same skill.

That is the sophisticated frame.

Best line to add

It may be better at making things occupy space than making things earn attention.

Or:

It looks stronger at geometry than taste.

Or:

The model can construct, but it still does not quite compose.

Best:

GPT‑5.6 may be better at spatial construction than product judgment.

Missing elements to add

Your post would be much stronger if it included these distinctions:

Missing elementWhy it mattersSuggested wordingConfirmation statusAvoids overclaiming a leak“Unconfirmed until OpenAI posts it.”SurfaceChatGPT? API? Codex? mobile?“Unknown whether this is ChatGPT, API, or staged rollout.”Test typeMakes claim more credible“In early visual/spatial tests…”Narrow comparisonPrevents “beats Fable overall?” replies“In some 3D/spatial tasks, not overall.”Frontend definitionMakes critique useful“Taste, spacing, hierarchy, responsive states.”Personal usageGives practical value“I’ll use it for 3D/procedural assets, not final frontend.”Vacation note separationKeeps credibilityPut it at the end, after the insight.

Better benchmark language

Instead of:

In some areas like 3D modeling, it’s surpassing even Claude Fable 5.

Say:

In early 3D-style scene and geometry tests, GPT‑5.6 looks unusually strong — possibly ahead of Fable 5 in that narrow lane.

Instead of:

frontend issues

Say:

frontend taste and product coherence

Instead of:

I’ll definitely be using it a lot

Say:

I expect to use it heavily for spatial prototyping, SVG/geometry work, and asset ideation.

A better “what I’ll use it for” section

Add this:

My likely use cases:3D scene ideation
SVG and geometry generation
Three.js prototypes
Blender/Python asset scaffolds
visual reference decomposition
spatial layouts and diagrams
quick mock assets for games/products
What I probably will not trust it with yet: final frontend taste, polished landing pages, design systems, mobile states, or brand-sensitive product UI.

This gives the post practical weight.

The “frontend is not code” angle

This is the strongest critique.

Frontend is not just generating React. Frontend is taste under constraints.

A model can be good at writing components and still bad at frontend because frontend requires:

choosing what not to show
visual rhythm
hierarchy
affordance
responsive judgment
state design
accessibility
performance
product intent
brand context
user expectation

Suggested paragraph:

The mistake people make is treating frontend as a coding task. It is partly code, but the hard part is judgment. The layout has to know what matters. The interaction has to know what the user is trying to do. The page has to feel intentional. Models still often produce UI that is functional but spiritually empty.

That is excellent if you want the post to feel smarter.

The “3D vs frontend” contrast

Use this:

3D generation rewards explicit structure. Frontend rewards implicit taste.

Or:

Geometry can be specified. Taste has to be inferred.

Or:

A 3D object can be correct in space. A frontend has to be correct in context.

Best:

A 3D scene can be judged by structure. A product UI has to be judged by intent.

Stronger caveat on “coming in a few days”
Since today is Friday, June 19, 2026, “in a few days” is vague. If you mean next week, say the date or window.
Options:
expected next week
expected within the next few days
possibly landing the week of June 22
rumored for late June
maybe as soon as next week
Best:
GPT‑5.6 / GPT‑5.6 Pro are rumored for late June, possibly within days.
That gives you more room if the rollout slips.
Stronger comparison against Fable
Use this if you want to mention Fable without inviting an argument:

Fable 5 still feels like the better reference point for long-horizon coding and agentic product work, but GPT‑5.6 may be catching or passing it in specific visual/spatial outputs.

That is consistent with Anthropic’s own positioning of Fable 5 as a long-horizon coding/agentic model.

“What would make me change my mind?” section

This is a high-credibility addition:

I’ll change my mind on frontend if it can consistently do three things:match a real design reference without destroying spacing;
inspect the rendered page and fix visual mismatches;
produce interfaces that feel product-led, not template-led.

That is much stronger than “frontend bad.”

Test protocol you can mention

For a future post:

My frontend test will be simple: give it a strong design reference, ask for a responsive implementation, make it inspect browser screenshots at desktop/tablet/mobile, then see whether it can fix the visual mismatches without turning the UI generic.

For 3D:

My 3D test will be: ask for a coherent isometric scene, a Three.js object hierarchy, a Blender script, and a complex SVG with labels, depth, occlusion, shadows and consistent perspective.

For games:

My game test will be: can it generate stable visuals, collisions, state transitions, restart logic and responsive controls without visual glitches?

Possible final post with more authority

GPT‑5.6 / GPT‑5.6 Pro are rumored to be close.The interesting part is where the improvement seems to be. Early signals suggest a big jump in visual/spatial work: 3D-style scene construction, SVG/geometry, procedural assets and structured visual generation. In some narrow tests, it may even be stronger than Fable 5.But I’m less convinced on frontend. It may generate cleaner code, but the same deeper issues seem to remain: taste, hierarchy, spacing, responsive polish, interaction states and making a UI feel like a real product instead of a competent https://t.co/D9bukOxwEy read: GPT‑5.6 may be much better at spatial construction than product judgment.I’ll probably use it heavily for 3D/procedural/visual work, but I’m not expecting it to replace the best frontend models yet.Back from vacation soon — sorry for the pause :)

The code may improve, but the taste problem remains: spacing, hierarchy, responsive states, product feel, and UI that looks designed rather than https://t.co/hVfDNKS38c my current take is simple: GPT‑5.6 may be better at building objects than designing products.I’ll test it properly when I’m back from vacation.
Best closing line
It may be stronger at geometry than taste — and frontend is mostly taste.

Best thread structure
Post 1
GPT‑5.6 / GPT‑5.6 Pro may be only days away. Still unconfirmed until it appears in OpenAI’s release notes, model picker, or API docs.
Post 2
The early signal I’m most interested in is not general reasoning. It is visual/spatial construction: 3D-style scenes, geometry, SVGs, procedural assets and image-to-structure tasks.
Post 3

Post 4

The disappointment is frontend. It still seems to struggle with the things that separate working code from good product: taste, layout rhythm, hierarchy, responsive behaviour, states, restraint and visual coherence.

Post 5

That distinction matters. A model can be excellent at constructing objects and still mediocre at designing interfaces.

Post 6

My current read: GPT‑5.6 Pro may be a major upgrade for visual construction, not yet a frontend taste breakthrough.

Post 7

I’ll test it properly when I’m back from vacation. Sorry for the pause :)

The “genius-level” angle

The real point is not model rankings. It is a distinction most people are missing:

Spatial intelligence and product taste are different capabilities.

A model can improve dramatically at:

geometry, perspective, object consistency, shape construction, scene decomposition, procedural structure

while still failing at:

design hierarchy, restraint, interaction logic, affordances, information architecture, visual rhythm, brand feel, product judgment

Suggested paragraph:

GPT‑5.6 may be exposing a useful split in model capability. It can get better at spatial construction without getting equally better at product design. A 3D asset has geometry problems. It may be better at making things occupy space than making things earn attention.

The model can construct, but it still does not quite compose.

In early 3D-style scene and geometry tests, GPT‑5.6 looks unusually strong — possibly ahead of Fable 5 in that narrow lane.

I expect to use it heavily for spatial prototyping, SVG/geometry work, and asset ideation.

The “frontend is not code” angle

This is the strongest critique.

Frontend is not just generating React. Frontend is taste under constraints.

A model can be good at writing components and still bad at frontend because frontend requires:

affordance
responsive judgment

accessibility

brand context

The mistake people make is treating frontend as a coding task. It is partly code, but the hard part is judgment. The layout has to know what matters. The interaction has to know what the user is trying to do. The page has to feel intentional. Models still often produce UI that is functional but spiritually empty.

That is excellent if you want the post to feel smarter.

The “3D vs frontend” contrast

Use this:

3D generation rewards explicit structure. Frontend rewards implicit taste.

Or:

Geometry can be specified. Taste has to be inferred.

Or:

A 3D object can be correct in space. A frontend has to be correct in context.

A 3D scene can be judged by structure. A product UI has to be judged by intent.

author: rekkusan0
text:
おはようございます。穏やかな日曜日、いかがお過ごしですか？

大切な人と過ごす週末のタイムラインですが、米政府の緊急指令や巨大テックのセキュリティ動向から、これまでの「クラウドAIに全てを丸投げする」という常識の危険性と、僕たちが今朝取るべき『現実的なデータ防衛策』を示す、決定的な事実が確定しました。

・@AnthropicAI：🚨【米政府が強制介入、過去最高知能『Claude Fable 5』を全世界で突如完全停止】先週リリースされた最上位知能に対し、トランプ政権（商務省）が安全保障を理由に輸出規制指令を発動。Amazon研究者がFable 5を使いサイバー攻撃に利用可能な情報を入手できたという実証結果が引き金となり、Amazonのジャシーが財務長官ベッセント氏に懸念を伝達したことが背景にある。同社は急遽、全地域・全ユーザー対象にFable 5とMythos 5を完全オフライン化する措置を余儀なくされた。Anthropicは「大きな誤解だ」と強く反論しているが、AI業界初の公開展開済みモデルへの政府介入という歴史的事例となった。

・@cursor ＆ @OpenRouter：🛡️【インフラ遮断に対抗する『知能の保険』の完全定着】政府介入によるFable 5の突然の停止を背景に、Cursorと専用エンドポイント（/api/v1/cursor）経由でOpenRouterに接続する分散ルーティングの実需が急騰。60以上のプロバイダーへの自動フェイルオーバーがデフォルトで有効化されており、特定のAIがダウンした際に裏側で即座に別のプロバイダへ切り替わる「自動フェイルオーバー」が必須の防衛ラインとなっている。

・@Microsoft ＆ @google：🏢【内製モデルの段階的統合と、開発環境の急速な変化】MicrosoftがBuild 2026（6月2日）でMAIファミリー7モデルを発表し、GitHub CopilotやVS Codeへの段階的統合（Project Polaris・8月移行予定）を本格化している。ただし「強制統合」ではなく段階的ロールアウトであり、OpenAI・Anthropicのモデルも引き続きFoundry上でホストされている。GoogleもGemini 3.5 Flash・Antigravity 2.0・Information Agentsと矢継ぎ早に展開を進めており、開発環境の急速な変化への対応が求められている。

・@xAI：📊【史上最大規模のSpaceX IPOとインフラ主権の確立】Grokを統合したSpaceXが6月12日にNasdaqへ上場し、終値161ドル（+19%）で時価総額約2.1兆ドル（約315兆円）を記録した。SpaceXはAnthropicとのColossus契約（月12億5,000万ドル・2029年5月まで・総額約387億ドル）とGoogleとのCloud SA契約（月9億2,000万ドル・2029年6月まで・総額約294億ドル）を通じ、競合するAI企業へのインフラ貸し出しという「インフラ側の主権」を確立している。MetaについてはEUのデジタル市場法（DMA）に基づく規制審査が継続しており、外部データの活用をめぐる法的圧力が高まっている。

・@OpenAI：📉【エージェントへの資源集中とIPOへのカウントダウン】6月8日にSECへの機密S-1提出を公式宣言したOpenAIが、Ona（旧Gitpod）の買収合意（規制当局承認待ち）により24時間常時稼働する自律エージェント基盤の内製化を加速している。月間10億ユーザーを背景にIPO時の目標評価額は1兆ドル超（約150兆円以上）とされており、公的市場からの大規模資金調達フェーズへ突入した。

author: readtw271
authorName: 海外华人青少年成长AI创业独角兽家长亲历By晓兵
text:
关于 GLM-5.2

Claude (opus 4.8 high ) : 

一句话:美国没有模型层面的”根本优势”,只有一个正在泄漏的领先,加上几条不在模型本身的真护城河。

核心逻辑链:

领先 ≠ 护城河。 SWE-bench 上美国只领先约三个点且在收窄,差距收窄的引擎是算法效率——而效率在开放研究里扩散最快,封不住。

模型层正在商品化。 中国用 MIT 开源 + 十倍便宜主动把模型变成大宗商品。一旦商品化,前沿那点能力差在商业上就不值钱了。

前沿在泄漏。 GLM 半数概率自称 Claude,是蒸馏指纹——美国花几十亿探的前沿,跟随者用零头蒸馏走九成。闭源是个漏桶。

出口管制双刃且可能反噬。 GLM-5 跑在十万颗昇腾、零英伟达,且在 Fable/Mythos 关停 48 小时后甩出 5.2。卡点不消灭对手,招来绕行——你越捏,对方自立越快。

美国真正耐久的优势全在模型之外: 供应链卡点(在被侵蚀)、资本与宏观吸纳力(是金融优势不是技术优势)、应用集成层与企业分发(护城河在 workflow 不在 weights)。

结论: 把战略目标定成”在跑分上不被超越”是看错棋盘。真正会让美国输的不是更强的中国模型,而是 ① 商品化抽干供养前沿的利润,② 管制亲手替对手锻造出供应链独立。该守的是模型的上下游,不是模型本身。

(折现提醒:GLM-5.2 发布时无官方基准,独立评测还没出;且它部分能力是蒸馏”借”来的,自主探前沿的成本中国这边还没真正付过。)

author.name: 海外华人青少年成长AI创业独角兽家长亲历By晓兵

quotedTweet.text:
“After using GLM-5.2 for a day, I’m surprised by how often it feels close to Opus 4.8/GPT-5.5 level.

I compared it side by side with Opus 4.8, and sometimes I even preferred GLM-5.2’s results.

OSS LLMs are impressive, especially given how many fewer GPUs they were trained on.” 美国大语言模型的根本优势何在？如何能够不被中国大语言模型超越？

Claude ( Opus 4.8 high) :
先把你引用那条推文背后的事实坐标钉牢,因为它本身就是论点的一半。

GLM-5 系列最刺眼的地方不是分数,而是它的训练底座:GLM-5 完全在国产华为昇腾芯片上训练,Zhipu 称之为”中国走向自主 AI 基础设施的里程碑” ￼——约十万颗昇腾 910B,零英伟达 ￼。而 GLM-5.2 在 6 月 13 日发布,正好是美国出口新规逼 Anthropic 对外籍用户关停 Fable 5 / Mythos 5 之后 48 小时 ￼。这个时间差不是巧合,是一句姿态宣言。所以你那位推主”用更少 GPU”的惊叹,其实低估了真正的新闻:不是更少英伟达,是没有英伟达。

带着这个事实,我对你这个问题的提法本身要先顶一下。

“根本优势”这个词可能是个伪命题。 美国现在有的是 lead(领先),不是 moat(护城河)。领先是快照,护城河是结构。把两者混为一谈,正是华盛顿出口管制思路的认知错误。模型层面的领先,今天具体值多少?SWE-bench Verified 上 GLM-5 是 77.8%,Opus 4.5 是 80.9%,GPT-5.2 是 80.0% ￼——三个点,且在收窄。而 GLM-5.1 到 5 的 28% 编码提升完全来自后训练,同一个底座,靠的是 slime 异步 RL 基础设施 ￼。也就是说,差距收窄的引擎是算法效率,而算法效率恰恰是开放研究里扩散最快的东西。你封不住论文,也封不住一个想法。

要回答你的问题,得先把”被超越”拆成四个不同的层,因为美国在每一层的处境完全不同:

一、前沿能力(谁先训出下一个最强的)。 美国仍领先,但这是跑步机不是护城河。原因有一个很脏但很关键的事实:GLM 系列在非常规探测下约 50% 的概率自称是 Claude,DeepSeek 也曾自称 ChatGPT ￼。这是蒸馏的指纹。它两头都割:一方面戳破”人家用零头算力就做到了”的神话——前沿那部分最贵的 R&D 是美国出钱探的;另一方面,它暴露了美国闭源商业模式的结构性漏桶——你花几十亿把前沿往前推,快速跟随者用一小笔钱蒸馏走九成。前沿在泄漏。这正是模型层注定商品化的微观机制。

二、单位算力/单位美元的能力(效率)。 这一层中国可能已经领先,而且是被逼出来的。这是你熟悉的霍尔木兹逻辑:卡点(chokepoint)不消灭对手,它招来绕行方案。出口管制没有冻结中国,它制造了 DeepSeek 的效率突破、slime、和昇腾的产业闭环。你越捏,对方的自给自足来得越快——管制在自我清算它本想守护的那个优势。

三、商业模式(这才是真正的不对称)。 中国在用 MIT 开源主动把模型层商品化。GLM-5.2 大约比 Claude / GPT-5 便宜十倍,MIT 许可,无地域限制,可自托管、可微调、可商用 ￼。如果模型是大宗商品,那美国在前沿的领先在商业上就不值钱了——除非那点能力差能撑得起十倍溢价。在大多数实际工作负载上撑不起。这是用开源把对手的利润池抽干的阳谋。

四、扩散与全球采用。 免费 + 便宜 + 无地域限制,赢的是全球南方和成本敏感型企业。美国闭源的溢价只在能力差足够大的高端场景成立。

那么美国真正相对耐久的优势在哪里?注意,几乎全都不在模型本身:

第一,算力供应链卡点——TSMC 先进制程、ASML、英伟达、CUDA。这是唯一真正的结构性筹码,但它正在被昇腾这件事侵蚀,而且双刃。这里有个值得你认真对待的反方观点:让中国依赖美国栈(英伟达、CUDA),可能比逼它自立更能拖长美国的领先。从这个角度,出口管制在战略上可能是适得其反的——它把一个偶然优势(谁正好控制了供应链)误当成可以靠封锁固化的永久优势。

第二,资本深度与宏观吸纳力。这大概是最耐久的一条,而它是个金融优势,不是技术优势。前沿训练以十亿美元计,微软/谷歌/亚马逊/Meta 加上美国 VC 能以中国国内无法匹配的规模持续投入——尤其在你那套资产负债表衰退框架下:通缩、去杠杆、企业资本开支疲软、地方财政吃紧。Zhipu IPO 募了约 5.58 亿美元、市值约 440 亿 ￼,真实,但相对于美国超大厂的投入是个零头。中国 AI 实验室在资本上被约束的程度,是美国实验室没有的。

第三,应用与集成层、企业分发与可信度。如果模型商品化,价值就上移到不商品化的层——这正是你 RCM 世界里的直觉:护城河在 workflow,不在 weights。Epic、合规信任、企业软件版图、API 生态——这一层美国结构性地强。

所以,回到你的提法”如何不被超越”,我的回答是:这个目标设定本身可能是错的。

如果”超越”指前沿能力——你只能靠砸更多算力、永远先推出下一个,来保持领先。但这是跑步机:因为泄漏(蒸馏)和效率扩散(开放研究),每一轮要花更多钱换更少的相对优势。你阻止不了被复制,只能跑得更快,而这越来越不划算。

如果”超越”指商业与经济主导——美国”赢”不靠拥有最聪明的模型,而靠在不商品化的层上攫取价值:供应链卡点(只要还守得住)、集成应用层、可信企业分发、以及为前沿融资和大规模部署的宏观能力。这条务实的路线,基本与跑分无关。

真正能让美国”输”的,从来不是一个更强的中国模型。是两件事:一,模型层商品化侵蚀掉那份供养前沿的经济回报;二,出口管制反噬,亲手替对手锻造出供应链独立性。GLM-5 跑在十万颗昇腾上、并在管制落地 48 小时后甩出 5.2,这两件事正在你眼前同时发生。

一句话:美国没有模型层面的”根本优势”,只有一个正在泄漏的领先和几条位于模型上下游、性质各异的真护城河。把战略目标定成”在 SWE-bench 上不被超越”,恰恰是看错了棋盘。

(顺带一个证伪自己的提醒:我对 GLM-5.2 的判断很大程度上建立在 Zhipu 自报和早期上手测试上——发布时官方没出基准,独立评测要再等两三周 ￼。蒸馏的 50% 自称 Claude 也提示,它的部分能力是”借”来的,真正自主探索前沿的成本还没由中国这边付过。这两点都该计入你对”差距”的折现里。)

author: lifeisameeme
text:
🚀为什么GLM 5.2 能直接干翻 Claude！   

在 Design Arena 的网页设计（单轮非代理）榜单上登顶第一！  它不仅把前代 GLM-5.1 提升了 5 名，还超越了 Claude Fable 5、Opus 4.6/4.7 等长期霸榜的闭源模型。  

Design Arena 官方揭秘了测试过程和 GLM 胜出的原因：
• 用更强模板 + 熟练调用 Tailwind、Chart.js、Three.js 等库，避开常见错误
• 生成的网站更精致、更有动画和细节（营销落地页特别强）
• 但生成时间是 Fable 5 的约 2 倍（更复杂 = 更慢）

5.2 这波绝对是开放模型对闭源的重大冲击！ 👏

author: rentierdigital
text:
fable 5 went offline in 12 hours. no deprecation window. no migration path. entire production pipeline dependent on 1 frontier model, and 1 government letter killed it globally.

the real move wasn't finding the next best model on the leaderboard. it was asking: what were we actually buying by routing everything through a single oracle?

turns out, something structurally better exists.

a panel of models with role diversity (security architect, skeptical economist, systems historian) plus a frontier judge synthesizing their disagreements scored 69.0% on DRACO deep research benchmarks. fable 5 solo scored 65.3%. the budget panel (gemini 3 flash, kimi k2.6, deepseek v4 pro) scored 64.7% at 40% of the cost.

the insight buried in those numbers: the architecture of deliberation outperforms the intelligence of any individual voice. management figured this out decades ago (committees, red teams, peer review). ai development spent 5 years chasing smarter single models without asking whether 3 medium-capable systems forced into structured disagreement might outperform 1 exceptional one uncontested.

turns out they might.

the perspective council stacks model diversity and role diversity at the same time. each panelist gets a different expert persona. the judge reads all responses, notes agreements and contradictions, synthesizes from the pattern. slower than a sprint. generally more right.

i build and ship daily. Claude Code, Codex, whatever ships fastest. SaaS, tools, automations. ⭐ if AI can build it, i've probably broken it first. what works → link in bio

author: zubiqo
text:
NEW: 🔬 OpenRouter Fuses Cheap Models to Mimic Fable 5

OpenRouter has launched Fusion, an API that runs prompts across multiple cheaper AI models simultaneously and synthesizes the outputs to rival expensive frontier models. The launch comes immediately after Anthropic suspended its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models for foreign nationals worldwide due to a U.S. export control directive.

Fusion sends queries to a panel of parallel models equipped with web search and bash tools, using a judge model to extract consensus and a Claude Opus 4.8 synthesizer to compile the final answer.

On Perplexity’s DRACO deep research benchmark, a cheap mixture of Gemini 3 Flash, Kimi K2.6, and DeepSeek V4 Pro synthesized by Opus scored 64.7%.

This multi-model combination beat solo GPT-5.5 at 60% and solo Opus 4.8 at 58.8%, finishing within a point of solo Fable 5 at 65.3% for approximately half the cost.

OpenRouter acknowledged that Fusion cannot fully replace Fable 5, as it underperforms on long-horizon tasks and cannot act as a wholesale swap for complex coding.

"A way bigger deal than it seems." — Andrew Trask

Frontier labs lose their absolute moat when clever server-side orchestration achieves comparable reasoning benchmarks for a fraction of the price. However, needing to manually patch the system to stop web-searching models from scraping the evaluation rubric shows how fragile these synthetic stacks can be.

Source: Decrypt

author: msresjudicata
text:
security standards

The White House and Anthropic PBC are discussing new standards for evaluating security flaws in advanced artificial intelligence models, Politico reported on Thursday, citing administration officials.
Officials are seeking a common method for assessing vulnerabilities known as "jailbreaks," which allow users to bypass an AI model's safeguards. According to the report, the framework could help determine the severity of future incidents and when government intervention may be necessary.
The talks come as Anthropic seeks to lift restrictions on its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models. The discussions follow a dispute over a security flaw in the company's latest AI systems that led Washington to impose export controls and restrict access for foreign users.

author: atmapshock
text:
US Government AI Model Export Controls and Cybersecurity Industry Operational Constraints: Policy Alignment Assessment

The US government's June 12 directive marked the first time Washington explicitly limited the release of a frontier AI model, and the industry response has exposed a structural fault line in how export control architecture applies to dual-use AI. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security directed Anthropic to suspend access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for any foreign national, whether inside or outside the United States, including Anthropic's own employees, forcing the company to disable both models for all customers to ensure compliance. A coordinated open letter from more than a hundred senior security practitioners argues the move harms defenders more than attackers. The interplay between export control objectives and operational security tooling needs is not marginal: the Mythos models were already demonstrating measurable defensive value, and their sudden withdrawal creates a capability gap that adversaries, unconstrained by the same directive, do not face.
https://t.co/sIHvkDawCc

author: guunyn8nl
text:
3am. One monitor. Four projects running at once.

Looks like chaos. It’s actually a pipeline where AI holds context while you switch lanes.

The breakdown:

Tab 1: app design. Claude generates the mockup backgrounds, accent color, headline font, icons sized for the Dynamic Island. One prompt, full pass.

Tab 2: doc review. Claude reads the draft, cuts the fluff, leaves two lines instead of a paragraph: “Driven by data, not vibes.”

Tab 3: debug. Claude reads a 200+ line leaderboard file first, before touching anything. No guessing. Read, then edit.

Tab 4: iPhone simulator. The build installs live while you’re still editing copy in another window.

No task waits on another.

The numbers: one builder running 3–4 parallel tracks instead of one. Review time drops from hours to minutes. The loop of “write it → see it on the phone” takes seconds, not a CI pipeline run.

Most people work one task at a time and wait for their head to clear. The edge goes to the one who lets AI hold context across four windows at once you’re not tracking everything in memory, you’re just tracking tempo.

While everyone else waits for one task to finish, the one running four wins.

Save this post. Get a second monitor and start parallel-tracking today.

author: cogan
text:
GLM 5.2 is absolutely a moment.

I’m using it as a coding agent through an API, not locally, and the results are remarkable. Frontier-level enough that I’d seriously consider it as the primary model behind an agent. And it costs far less than the closed frontier.

But Greg’s last line is the important one: "2027 is probably the year of local AI."

Because local frontier AI is not really here for most people today.

Yes, you can download the weights. Yes, you can run it yourself. But running a model this large well still requires an extraordinary amount of memory and accelerator hardware. The cost puts it outside the reach of almost everyone. Not to mention how difficult it is to even source the necessary hardware specs right now even if you have the capital to outlay.

That doesn’t diminish the moment. It defines it.

The model exists. The capability is here. The hardware just hasn’t caught up for the mass market yet.

But models are getting more efficient. Quantization is improving. Hardware will improve. Frontier-class intelligence will move onto machines ordinary people can actually own. That's why I appreciate Greg's directional 2027 caveat.

And after the Fable fiasco, the importance of that is impossible to miss.

We need open-weight models that cannot be switched off because a company, government, policy change, or geopolitical dispute says so.

We need intelligence we can possess, not merely rent.

GLM 5.2 is not that future for the average person yet.

But it makes that future feel considerably closer.

And I suspect that makes the closed frontier labs very nervous.

author: patrickojo_
text:
Last week the US government disabled Fable 5 and Mythos 5 overnight with no warning.

This week GLM-5.2 shows you can run a model matching that capability tier locally, on hardware you own, with no dependency on anyone’s export control directive, terms of service, or pricing decision.

The timing could not make the argument more clearly. Frontier-adjacent capability is no longer locked behind a small number of labs with kill-switch power. The companies building sovereign inference into their architecture right now are the ones who won’t be disrupted next time this happens, and there will be a next time.

author: hui1231123
text:
Claude Mythos shipped this month. The US just suspended export access to it.

So as a solo dev I won't touch the frontier for months. Fine — next week I'm running the opposite experiment:

Can I ship a real Unity feature using only the cheap workhorse models everyone has access to?
Budget cap: $5 for the week. Same project. Same scope. Full diary.

The thesis: 90% of indie gamedev never needed Mythos in the first place. Time to prove it.

👉 Follow for the day-by-day. I'll post the wall I hit and the workaround — or admit it can't be done.
